title: Humanoid robot masters ladders and obstacles with new approach
content: Researchers at ETH Zurich and collaborators developed a control approach that lets a humanoid robot climb ladders, cross obstacles, and recover from falls using a single learned policy.The system was demonstrated on Unitree’s G1 humanoid robot, showing how one approach can support different challenging movements. The method focuses on planning contact with the environment, rather than prescribing every movement in advance.In simulations, the approach achieved higher success rates than a comparison method across eight obstacle courses, highlighting its potential for improving humanoid robot mobility.Humanoid contact planningThe new system lets a humanoid robot climb ladders, cross obstacles, crawl through confined spaces, and recover from falls using a single learned policy.The technology, called Attention-based Contact Planning (ACP), helps the robot decide where to place its hands, feet, knees, elbows, and pelvis against the surrounding environment.The system was tested on Unitree’s G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating how contact planning and reinforcement learning can help robots adapt their movements to different terrain without following predefined motion sequences.With @JayHe748646 @KehanWen170077 @leggedrobotics , we push humanoid mobility to next frontier.Achieved by a generalist contact planner + a generalist tracker + a generalized neural mapping, warmstarted from few human data.Website: https://t.co/Y7cu3D4K4IPromo Video 👇 pic.twitter.com/ouZQskpZmQ— C. Zhang (@ChongZzZhang) October 23, 2026ACP combines reinforcement learning with motion imitation to address challenges in whole-body robot control. Reinforcement learning allows robots to improve through repeated attempts and feedback, while motion imitation teaches them to follow recorded movements. However, reinforcement learning can struggle with complex coordination, and imitation-based systems may struggle to adapt to unfamiliar obstacles.According to the team, instead of generating a complete sequence of body movements, ACP predicts suitable contact points on the surrounding terrain. A separate controller then coordinates the robot’s joints to reach those points.For example, when climbing a ladder, the robot must identify suitable rungs for its hands and feet. Its controller then coordinates its arms, legs, and torso to move between those points while maintaining support. The approach allows the robot to adapt its movements without following a fixed climbing sequence.The contact planner uses an attention-based neural network to process terrain information, the robot’s internal state, and a user-provided goal. Its inputs include joint positions, joint velocities, and body orientation. The system plans contacts for nine body parts: two hands, two elbows, two knees, two feet, and the pelvis. This allows the robot to use its upper body for support when walking alone is insufficient.Robots navigate obstaclesThe researchers also developed a LiDAR-based mapping system that converts sensor measurements into a local height map and estimates their reliability. This helps the robot identify narrow surfaces, such as ladder rungs, that might otherwise be missed. Running on a Jetson Orin NX computer, the system processes a 20,000-point LiDAR scan in 30 milliseconds, updating scans at 10 Hz.Researchers say the training took place in three stages. First, a whole-body controller learned to execute contact plans using 13.2 minutes of human motion data adapted to the robot’s body structure and physical limits. Next, the researchers trained the contact planner and controller together. Finally, reinforcement learning helped the system adapt to procedurally generated environments beyond the original demonstrations. Successful attempts provided additional training examples.During deployment, the robot does not need reference motions. It uses onboard observations and a specified goal to plan contacts and generate movements.Real-world demonstrations showed the G1 climbing ladders and stairs, crossing stepping stones, crawling, vaulting over obstacles, and recovering after falls. In simulations, the system achieved an average success rate of 92.5 percent across eight composite obstacle courses, compared with 58.8 percent for the MGMT baseline, a motion-generation-and-tracking approach. These figures represent simulated performance, not real-world success rates.The researchers note that the system currently focuses on terrain-based interactions and local movement toward a goal. Tasks involving overhead contacts, hanging, and manipulation would require more advanced three-dimensional perception.

title: 10,300-ton USS Pinckney warship gets advanced SPY-6 radar upgrade
content: The U.S. Navy’s USS Pinckney has entered a San Diego shipyard to begin installing the service’s first SPY-6(V)4 radar on an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer. The modernization work began at General Dynamics NASSCO and will equip the warship with upgraded sensors and cooling systems to counter evolving missile and aerial threats.This project is the second phase of the Destroyer Modernization 2.0 program, which aims to boost the combat abilities of four guided-missile destroyers. The $149.6 million contract is set to wrap up by September 2028.A new radar for advanced threat detectionThe main part of the upgrade is Raytheon’s AN/SPY-6(V)4 radar, which will help the Navy better detect and track aerial threats. The system will be integrated with the Aegis Combat System Baseline 10, so the destroyer can handle both air and ballistic missile defense at the same time.The new radar will help Pinckney respond to more advanced weapons, such as incoming missiles and drones. This is especially important because Navy destroyers operate in areas where ships and commercial vessels face greater security threats.The upgrade also brings in new High Efficiency Super-Capacity air conditioning systems. These will help handle the extra electrical and heat demands from the new combat equipment.“The collective effort by all stakeholders has finally brought us to the point of execution,” said Capt. Tim Moore, program manager for DDG MOD 2.0. “Upon Depot Modernization Period completion, USS Pinckney will rejoin the Fleet equipped with the most comprehensive multi-spectral integrated sensor suite designed to maintain maritime superiority for decades to come.”Building on earlier electronic warfare upgradesThe USS Pinckney has a displacement of approximately 10,300 US short tons (9,300 metric tonnes). Pinckney finished its first modernization period, called DMP 1.5, in 2024. At that time, it was the first warship to get the SLQ-32(V)7 Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program Block III system and structural sponson changes.The electronic warfare system helps the ship find and respond to electronic threats. The Navy used a step-by-step installation method, called Split Start, so industry partners could gain experience with the upgrades before moving on to the radar installation.After the earlier upgrades, Pinckney spent eight and a half months deployed in the Pacific and Middle East. The Navy said this deployment proved the destroyer’s advanced warfare abilities in challenging environments.Four destroyers support the modernization programThe DDG MOD 2.0 program includes four Arleigh Burke-class destroyers: USS Pinckney (DDG 91), USS Chung-Hoon (DDG 93), USS James E. Williams (DDG 95), and USS Halsey (DDG 97).These ships are getting electronic warfare upgrades before their radar upgrades. This gives the Navy and its industry partners experience for future projects.The Navy plans to combine modernization work for future ships. USS Sterett (DDG 104) will likely be the first to get both upgrades done in a single shipyard visit.Shorter shipyard periods could improve fleet readinessCombining upgrades into a single shipyard period could reduce the time destroyers spend out of service. The approach would also help the Navy modernize more ships while maintaining operational availability.These upgrades come as U.S. naval forces face more demands in the Indo-Pacific and Middle East. Destroyers are key to protecting carrier strike groups and other ships from missile and drone attacks.By adding advanced radar and improved electronic warfare systems, the Navy wants its destroyers to detect and defend more effectively as threats to deployed ships keep changing.

title: US team turns everyday Mylar into promising lunar habitat insulation
content: Living on the Moon sounds fascinating, but of course it is not. The University of Pennsylvania has developed an insulating material designed for the harsh environments of long-term lunar missions.Dubbed hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS), the material combines high thermal insulation with mechanical durability. This kind of balance is rarely achieved by current space insulators like aerogels or standard multilayer insulation, which tend to be fragile or easily torn.HyLIFS consists of hundreds of stacked, ultrathin Mylar sheets (the polymer used in emergency space blankets). Some layers are coated with a thin layer of aluminum oxide (alumina) to enhance stiffness and block infrared radiation.Protecting the future explorersWhen the humans return to the Moon to stay, keeping warm won’t be easy. Lunar temperatures swing wildly, dropping hundreds of degrees below zero during the long night before spiking above boiling at noon. Space agencies mostly use lightweight insulators like aerogels and reflective foils to survive the vacuum of space, but they’re also exploring alternatives. Penn is working on hybrid layered insulating film stacks.Researchers created a highly durable insulator with top-tier thermal performance by stacking Mylar sheets coated in aluminum oxide. The material retains its protective insulating power even under extreme compressive pressure.“These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression, and maintain their insulating performance. Potentially allowing them to be packed, transported, and survive rough treatment over many years of use,” said Igor Bargatin, senior author and Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM). The material’s strength surprised even its creators. During lab testing, the thin stacks were repeatedly subjected to 20 megapascals of compressive stress. It is roughly equal to balancing 200 pounds on the tip of a single finger. The material survived across 10 consecutive stress cycles. “We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress. But the stacks didn’t survive just one high stress cycle — they survived 10 in a row,” said first author Danielle R. Levin. Role of antiblocking particlesIn solving the durability problem, the team also stumbled upon an unexpected scientific insight.It was originally assumed that using the thinnest available films would yield the best insulation. Thinner films allow more layers to be packed into the same space, fitting in a higher number of heat-blocking boundaries. The data proved otherwise.The key was in “antiblocking” particles, which are microscopic bumps added by commercial manufacturers to keep plastic wrap from sticking to itself. In a vacuum, heat doesn’t travel through the empty space between layers, but it crosses almost entirely through the microscopic contact points where these tiny particles touch neighboring sheets.A higher concentration of contact points in thinner films creates more pathways for heat to leak through. Through mapping the way these microscopic particles deform under pressure, the Penn team realized they could custom-design heat barriers by tuning particle size, film stiffness, and coating thickness. “The simplest configuration ended up being the best one,” noted Levin.The current prototype samples are small (about one square centimeter) and manually assembled sheet by sheet. Scaling the process up to produce meter-wide rolls for habitats, rovers, and spacesuits will require automated roll-coating manufacturing.The combination of flexibility, toughness, and low cost makes HyLIFS an attractive candidate for lunar habitats, spacesuits, rovers, and electronics that often endure accidental bumps, packing, and long-term space exposure.The findings were published in the journal ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces.

title: Silver additive helps new battery retain 90% capacity after 200 cycles
content: A team at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) has created a new battery design that could make future energy storage both lighter and longer-lasting. Their anode-free lithium metal battery reached an energy density of 467 Wh/kg (212 Wh/lb) in a pouch cell, bringing its performance closer to that of current commercial batteries.The full coin cell retained 90 percent of its capacity after 200 charge-discharge cycles. The results come from a strategy that modifies critical battery interfaces to improve lithium deposition and stabilize the internal layers that govern battery performance.Led by Professor Shao Minhua, the research team developed the approach to address persistent problems that limit the lifespan and energy density of anode-free lithium batteries.Anode-free design faces lithium deposition problemsLithium metal is a promising battery material because it has a high specific capacity and a low reduction potential. Anode-free batteries use a bare copper current collector instead of a separate anode to store lithium, reducing inactive material and simplifying manufacturing.However, conventional copper surfaces do not readily attract lithium. This can cause lithium to deposit unevenly during charging, encouraging the growth of dendrites, which are needle-like structures that can damage battery components and create safety risks.Another problem is the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), a layer that forms naturally on the electrode surface. When this layer becomes unstable, it can interfere with lithium-ion movement and shorten the battery’s life.Silver-based additive reshapes battery interfacesTo solve these problems, the researchers added an AMI additive with silver ions and anions. This additive starts several processes after the battery is put together, helping to change the copper surface and control how lithium is deposited.The silver-modified surface improves lithiophilicity, making it easier for lithium to deposit more evenly. It also anchors anion-derived species that help build a more stable SEI.The resulting interface has an organic-rich inner layer and an inorganic-rich outer layer. This arrangement is designed to support lithium-ion transport while limiting the conditions that encourage dendrite growth.Quasi-solid gel strengthens the protective layerThe released anions also start a reaction in the electrolyte that forms a quasi-solid gel inside the organic inner and inorganic outer SEI layers. This keeps the electrode and electrolyte in close contact, stabilizing the interface over many charge and discharge cycles.These changes help lithium plate and strip more reversibly, so the battery wears less over time. The researchers also say this combined method can make batteries safer by stopping dendrites from forming.Integrated strategy could advance future batteriesShao, who is the corresponding author and head of HKUST’s Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, explained that this approach combines several functions into a single process.“The key is not simply adding a silver salt or a polymerization initiator. Our AMI releases multiple functions through a controlled process after cell assembly, allowing us to modify the current collector, build an anion-derived solvation structure, and form a robust organic-inner/inorganic-outer SEI in one integrated process,” he added.“This makes lithium plating and stripping highly reversible in an anode-free, quasi-solid-state configuration, laying a stronger foundation for the development of next-generation batteries.”The study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: Fukushima nuclear cleanup: How robots are removing radioactive debris
content: Robots are helping engineers tackle the complex cleanup of Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station by inspecting damaged reactors and surveying radioactive deposits. Hitachi has developed specialized robotic systems that can operate in confined spaces, underwater environments, and high-radiation areas, reducing the need for workers to enter hazardous locations.One system, PMORPH, is a shape-changing crawler designed to inspect the reactor’s primary containment vessel and assess conditions inside. Another, HUMALT, uses flexible robotic arms to perform tasks in high-radiation environments, with potential applications in nuclear fuel debris retrieval.Recent reports suggest that more than 53,000 Fukushima cleanup workers have exceeded an annual radiation exposure of 5 millisieverts since 2011, with 17 occupational illnesses recognized.Probe radioactive reactorsPMORPH passes through a pipe approximately 10 centimeters in diameter in an I-shaped configuration before transforming into a U-shape inside the vessel.The first PMORPH unit entered the Unit 1 containment vessel in April 2015, using a camera, thermometer, and radiation dosimeter to examine conditions outside the reactor pedestal. A second version, deployed in March 2017, used a winch-lowered sensor unit to investigate submerged deposits and measure radiation levels on the basement floor.To examine these deposits more closely, Hitachi developed six types of underwater remotely operated vehicles (ROVs). They create three-dimensional maps of deposit surfaces, measure deposit thickness and radiation levels, prevent cable entanglement, and collect physical samples. During an investigation from February 2022 to March 2023, the vehicles gathered information needed to develop a method for recovering deposits inside the Unit 1 containment vessel.Hitachi has also developed the Telescopic Active Scope Camera (TASC) to access bent pipes and help remove contaminated water. At Unit 1, highly contaminated water inside a heat exchanger has raised radiation levels nearby.TASC uses short cilia covering a hose to propel itself through vibrations generated by a motor. Wheels at its tip control its direction, while an inner hose carries water out. An active scope camera allows operators to monitor conditions at the tip as the device navigates the piping.Tackle nuclear decommissioningAnother system, HUMALT, is a flexible robotic arm designed for high-radiation environments and potential fuel debris retrieval operations. Instead of placing radiation-sensitive electronic components throughout its body, it uses multiple cylinder-type water-hydraulic actuators to move its arm. Its joints combine bending and rotational movements, enabling controlled manipulation while reducing the likelihood of damage from contact with surrounding structures.The system uses water as its hydraulic fluid, limiting environmental impact if a line is damaged. Operators control it remotely through hose lines connected to a pump unit and control panel. A predecessor equipped with two flexible arms was deployed in Fukushima Daiichi’s Unit 3 turbine building in 2019 to remove obstacles.Radiation remains a major challenge for these machines. Hitachi uses radiation-resistant sensors, shielding, and designs that separate sensitive electronics from robot bodies. Components may also need replacement when they approach their accumulated radiation-dose limits.The company is developing automation for repetitive operations, such as rubble removal in areas with comparatively low radiation levels. For more complex tasks, operators continue to rely on remote control. Hitachi is also developing systems that use external stereo cameras to estimate the three-dimensional positions of robots, their surroundings, and their articulated arms when sensors cannot be mounted directly on the machines.Hitachi plans to combine these robotic platforms with artificial intelligence, sensor data, workers’ expertise, and digital twin technologies. The goal is to let robots assess their surroundings and perform instructed tasks with greater autonomy, while people supervise operations and make decisions when needed.By combining specialized hardware with remote operation and AI-assisted control, these systems could improve worker safety and help engineers tackle the complex, long-term process of nuclear decommissioning.

title: US method separates 90% copper from mixed metal powders for reuse
content: Researchers at the University of Maine have developed a new method to recover high-value metals, including copper and aluminum, from contaminated powder mixtures. This breakthrough could strengthen the country’s “Made in USA” manufacturing goals.These high-value materials are used to make precision-engineered parts, such as biomedical implants, aircraft components, battery materials, and cutting tools. Recognizing that material loss is a major challenge across critical sectors, the Maine researchers set out to address the issue.“We’re trying to solve a significant materials-loss problem that occurs during the production of high-value components and products across critical sectors, such as aerospace, energy storage, tooling, biomedical devices and electronics,” said Bashir Khoda, lead researcher and associate professor of mechanical engineering.He noted that the new procedure could make manufacturing more robust by helping address uncertainty in the supply chain for critical minerals, which affects cost, availability and production resilience.Spin to separateIn the study, researchers focused on recovering metals from powder mixtures that are often discarded because of cross-contamination during handling processes.Using a new method called shear-assisted particle entrapment (SHAPE), researchers mixed two critical metals in a liquid suspension. They placed the mixture in a spinning machine at variable speeds to separate the individual particles. The team then captured the isolated particles on a thin polymer film.During the experiments, the team tested aluminum and copper microparticles ranging from 0 to 25 micrometers in diameter. The team suspended the particle mixture in a liquid and exposed it to rotational speeds ranging from 200 to 1,500 revolutions per minute (rpm).At approximately 200 rpm, about 87 percent of the particles captured on the substrate were the lighter material, aluminum. As the rotational speed increased to 1,500 rpm, the dominant population shifted, with copper accounting for about 90 percent of the entrapped particles.The researchers said that by fine-tuning the process parameters, they could selectively capture different particles.Selective capture, low yieldsAlthough the laboratory demonstration achieved high particle-level selectivity, the yields recovered from the starting material remained very low.“The current study demonstrates the selectivity of the mechanism, rather than an industrially ready recovery process,” Khoda said. “The next challenge is to maintain this selectivity while substantially increasing the amount of material that can be processed and recovered.”Future work will examine substrate size and geometry, the use of multiple substrates, particle loading, polymer concentration, processing time, and continuous or multistage operation to increase the amount of material processed while maintaining selective separation.The team also plans to evaluate whether the recovered powders possess the properties required for reuse by examining their chemistry, morphology, flowability, and manufacturing performance.In the long term, the researchers aim to automate the process by integrating it with artificial intelligence.“Our longer-term objective is not simply to separate particles in the laboratory, but to develop a scalable and AI-driven manufacturing system that could recover cross-contaminated powders and return usable material to the additive manufacturing supply chain and beyond,” Khoda said.The findings were published in Powder Technology.

title: Supercurrent could reveal quantum information without destroying it
content: A collaborative research project between scientists at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil and the Beijing Institute of Technology in China has solved a long-pending problem in quantum technology: reading a qubit without destroying the information it contains. Their approach avoids the use of ancillas or auxiliary qubits that are used in non-destructive quantum readout methods too, making it quite a special feat. As quantum technologies advance, scientists are looking for ways to measure quantum bits, or qubits that store quantum information. The nature of qubits is that they can store a large number of values between 0 and 1 but are also extremely prone to external disturbances. While this property lets qubits store large amounts of information at once, the latter makes computations with that information error-prone. To minimize errors, one could read the information stored in the qubits from time to time, but this destroys or changes the information, presenting different challenges for researchers. To address this, scientists have developed non-destructive quantum measurement methods that typically involve ancillas or auxiliary qubits. These ancillas must be paired with the qubit, after which information is transferred and then read. This increases the time required and the complexity of the whole measurement process. So, a team led by Jose Carlos Euges at IFSC-USP and Yugui Yao at the Beijing Institute of Technology turned to Andreev qubits to determine if they could be measured directly. What are Andreev Qubits? Named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev, the Andreev qubits are a quantum characteristic of the interface between normal and superconducting materials. Also known as Andreev states, these occur in the nanoscale region between superconducting materials and can encode states like 0 and 1 and superpositions. A system has another phenomenon called supercurrent, where electric current flows without any resistance. The researchers incorporated an Andreev qubit in a closed superconducting circuit and placed a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) near it to measure changes in weak magnetic fields. When supercurrent flows through the circuit, the SQUID can measure the changes in the magnetic field and determine how the current is behaving. The researchers also found that the supercurrent has two components, a constant one and a fluctuating one. Measuring these components reveals the proportion of states 0 and 1 contributing to the superposition, while the other reveals their phase relationship. Knowing these is equivalent to knowing the state of the qubit. Reading without destroying“We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID senses that field,” explained Egues in a press release. “Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”Quantum measurements always change the information on the qubit, and this time too; it’s no different. The device the team is proposing will give feedback that will alter the state of the qubit. However, in the team’s simulations, these state changes are so small that they are irrelevant. With accuracies of 99.52 percent, 99.81 percent, and 99.85 percent, the results are within the limits of the margin of error. “Our method doesn’t eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits – the ancillas – employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols,” added Egues. Moreover, the approach allows the researchers to work without resetting the qubit to its initial state, which could help develop more advanced systems in the near future. The researchers published the findings in Physical Review B.

title: Could Japan's space agency be the first to finally bring a Mars sample home?
content:
Now that NASA’s Mars Sample Return mission is on ice, Japanese space agency JAXA’s Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission may be our best chance of seeing a Martian rock sample returned to Earth within the next decade.
This is largely down to the relative simplicity of MMX compared to NASA’s scrapped sample return plans. Instead of landing on the Red Planet, MMX is sending a spacecraft to Mars’ moon Phobos. Once there, it will attempt to scrape some moon dust from the surface before returning it to Earth.

title: Flexible solar cells hit 26.86% efficiency in chemical breakthrough
content: A joint research team led by Southeast University and Soochow University has found a way to stop the molecular fighting in flexible perovskite solar cells. To turn rigid solar tech into bendable panels that can roll over backpacks or car roofs, researchers had to fix a major manufacturing flaw in flexible perovskite solar cells. Printing these flexible devices requires depositing two layers at once. A ultrathin foundational transport layer called a single-molecule film (self-assembled monolayer, SAM), and the light-harvesting perovskite crystalsWhen engineers tried to coat them together onto bendable substrates, the SAM molecules and perovskite components bound too strongly to each other instead of taking their proper positions. This chemical feud left behind uneven, defect-ridden layers that broke down under operational heat and humidity. The joint research team solved this chemical roadblock by introducing a customized “decoupling” molecule. The discovery acts as an atomic referee. It prevents the two components from reacting prematurely and unlocks reliable, large-scale production.“A 25-square-centimeter flexible device retained 92.5 percent of its initial PCE of 22 percent after 1044 hours of maximum power point tracking at 85°C (185°F) and 65 percent relative humidity,” the study paper noted. Fixing the problemFlexible substrates have uneven surface roughness and varying hydroxyl-group densities, making standard large-area printing techniques ineffective. Attempting a conventional co-deposition strategy improves surface wettability, yet strong intermolecular interactions between transport layer molecules and perovskite components disrupt both substrate anchoring and crystal formation. These chemical conflicts ultimately leave current flexible solar modules far behind their rigid counterparts in both efficiency and stability.Researchers introduced a “decoupled co-deposition” strategy to improve large-area flexible perovskite solar modules. The approach resolves the challenge of uniformly printing transport layers and perovskite films onto flexible substrates. It provides a practical chemical solution to boost both the conversion efficiency and operational stability of flexible solar devices. To fix the chemical interference, the research team added a decoupling modulator molecule featuring ammonium ions, iodide ions, and two sulfonate groups to the precursor solution. This additive forms strong chelating bonds with the perovskite framework. It blocks harmful interactions between transport layer molecules and perovskite components. With the interference removed, the transport molecules can quickly stick to the flexible base, while the new additive guides crystal growth and seals up flaws in the perovskite layer.Technique works well in testingThis strategy optimizes both the transport and perovskite layers together, driving efficiency and durability to record levels. The results hit record numbers. Small-area flexible cells achieved a third-party certified efficiency of 26.86 percent. Scaling up yielded record module efficiencies across the board: 22.31 percent for 5×5 cm² panels, 20.63 percent for 10×10 cm² panels, and 20.15 percent for large 30×30 cm² sheets.Durability held up under pressure too. The flexible modules survived thermal shock cycles from frigid lows to extreme heat and passed the rigorous IEC 63163 international stability standard.“More important, this strategy facilitates the modules to pass the industry-standard IEC 63163 stability series certification, providing an important foundation for the industrial development of flexible perovskite photovoltaics,” the team stated. This collaborative work delivers a new chemical strategy for fabricating high-performance flexible perovskite modules in China. Future research will focus on refining decoupling molecules, integrating tandem cell designs, and scaling production for roll-to-roll manufacturing. These developments support the modernization of renewable energy systems and help drive national carbon-reduction goals.The findings were published in the journal Science.

title: Guinness world record: Motorcycle skims across water for over 25 miles
content: A Chinese motorcycle entrepreneur has set a Guinness World Record by riding a modified motorcycle across open water for more than 25 miles (40 kilometers). The achievement took place in his hometown in Hunan Province and marked a milestone for the founder of motorcycle manufacturer ZXMOTO.Zhang Xue used a specially modified motorcycle to complete the record attempt, making repeated runs across a river to cover the required distance. The feat concludes a pursuit that began in 2009, when Zhang first experimented with riding a motorcycle on water and overcame early failures to achieve his latest goal.Motorcycle skims waterXue set a Guinness World Record for the longest distance traveled on open water by a modified motorcycle. The record attempt took place in Mayang Miao Autonomous County in central China’s Hunan Province, where Zhang repeatedly traveled back and forth across a river on a specially modified ZXMOTO MX450.The motorcycle was adapted to operate on land and water, with amphibious skis, an enlarged fuel tank, and added waterproofing. Its design allows it to build up speed on land before skimming across the water, with a front ski providing steering and the rear tire generating propulsion by pushing water backward.The MX450 featured several modifications to support its unusual operating conditions. Amphibious skis help the motorcycle remain above the water’s surface, while the front ski provides directional control during the crossing.The rear tire plays a different role from its conventional use on roads. Instead of relying on traction against a solid surface, it pushes water backward to generate forward propulsion. This allows the motorcycle to continue moving across the river after accelerating on land.The motorcycle operates differently from a conventional watercraft, which typically uses a dedicated propulsion system designed for aquatic environments. The modified MX450 instead relies on its rear tire and the interaction between its skis and the water surface.The team also enlarged the fuel tank and added waterproofing to prepare the motorcycle for repeated water exposure. These changes were intended to support the long-distance challenge, which required multiple crossings rather than a single uninterrupted run in one direction.From failure to recordThe record attempt followed years of experimentation with motorcycle-based water travel. Zhang first tried to ride a motorcycle across water in 2009, using basic modifications to explore whether the machine could remain moving on the surface.That early experiment proved difficult. Zhang fell into the water four times and achieved a maximum distance of only 20 meters (66 feet). Nevertheless, the initial attempt marked the beginning of a longer effort to develop a motorcycle configuration capable of traveling across water.The latest achievement demonstrates how modifications to a conventional motorcycle can change the conditions under which it operates. Rather than being limited to road surfaces, the adapted MX450 combines land-based acceleration with skis for water travel and tire-driven propulsion.However, the record does not establish that the configuration is suitable for ordinary motorcycle use on water or for routine amphibious transportation. The reported achievement concerns a specific modified motorcycle and a Guinness World Record attempt, rather than a commercially available vehicle designed for general-purpose travel across land and water.

title: US engineers use sound to identify catastrophic failures of drones
content:
Autonomous drone to use sound alone to detect damage
“The project started in 2024 with interest by NASA in detecting problems with motors before a drone took off,”
UC College of Engineering and Applied Science doctoral student Prissha Chawla. “More and more, drones are being used for public safety. You don’t want them to crash.”
Eventually, the students envision an autonomous drone that can use sound alone to detect damage to its own propellers and other mechanical
in flight so it can return to base before sustaining a catastrophic failure, according to a press release.
Besides chips or cracks in propellers, Chawla said grit and other debris can get into motor bearings, causing it to seize.
Damage-detection system could be a feature
“We’re focusing on pre-flight tests that NASA already runs,” she said.
UC student Luke Busse said the damage-detection system could be a feature of fully autonomous “drone-in-a-box” systems. Drones deploy from a weatherproof docking station that handles launch, landing, charging, data upload and mission scheduling without an on-site operator.
“In that scenario, it would be great. You could have sensors in the box that provide preflight checks,” Busse said.
Drone motors and propellers generate characteristic sounds during operation. When a component becomes damaged or begins to fail, these sounds can change, potentially providing an early indication of a mechanical problem.
The approach is particularly valuable because not every mechanical problem can be easily identified through a visual inspection. While a crack in a propeller may be visible, contamination inside a motor bearing can be more difficult to detect. According to the researchers, grit and other debris can enter motor bearings and cause them to seize, potentially resulting in a loss of propulsion.
Acoustic monitoring could therefore provide an additional layer of protection by identifying unusual mechanical behaviour that might otherwise go unnoticed during routine inspections.
The technology could be particularly useful in situations where drones operate frequently or perform missions with limited time for detailed manual checks. Detecting a fault before launch could prevent equipment damage, reduce operational interruptions, and help protect people and property on the ground.

title: Submarine torpedo strike sends frigate to bottom of sea in trial
content: Two countries have recently tested newly-made surface-to-surface guided missiles. Greek and Israeli naval forces conducted the acceptance firings of new Rafael-made missile systems. The trials of SPIKE NLOS and ER guided missiles were conducted on October 21 in the wider maritime area of the Northern Cretan Sea.The SPIKE guided missiles were successfully fired from a MACHITIS-class Gunboat and a MARK V Special Operations Craft, confirming the effectiveness and operational value of the new weapon system. Furthermore, cooperation with Israeli Navy vessels contributed to enhancing operational interoperability between the two Navies.Trial also included a torpedo firing from a submarineThe trial also included a torpedo firing from a submarine to sink decommissioned frigate HS MPOUMPOULINA (F-463). In addition, Israeli Navy units also conducted guided-missile firings.The Hellenic Navy’s first acceptance firing trials of the Israeli-made SPIKE NLOS and SPIKE ER2 guided missile systems showcased weapons’ power. The exercise took place in the northern Cretan Sea and brought together a wide range of Greek naval assets, air platforms and Israeli missile boats to demonstrate operational readiness and strengthen interoperability between the two navies.The event highlights Greece’s efforts to enhance its maritime strike capabilities while reinforcing its strategic partnership with Israel amid an increasingly complex security environment in the Eastern Mediterranean.Rafael-developed precision-guided weaponsThe missile firing trials involved two types of Rafael-developed precision-guided weapons. This included the SPIKE Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) missile and the SPIKE Extended Range (ER2) missile. Both systems were successfully launched from their designated platforms, demonstrating the operational value of the new installations.The SPIKE NLOS was fired from a Machitis-class patrol vessel, while the SPIKE ER2 was launched from a Mark V Special Operations Craft. These trials represent a significant step in bringing the new weapon systems into operational service with the Hellenic Navy.The SPIKE NLOS system provides a reported engagement range of up to 32 kilometres, enabling naval units to strike surface targets and support operations against coastal objectives. Its electro-optical and infrared guidance capabilities offer operational flexibility, including engagements against targets that may not be directly visible to the launching platform.Decommissioned Elli-class frigate was struck during guided missile trials The decommissioned Elli-class frigate was struck during the guided missile trials and subsequently sunk by an SUT torpedo fired from a Papanikolis-class Type 214HN submarine. The sequence demonstrated the ability of different naval weapon systems to participate in a coordinated engagement against a surface target.The sinking also highlighted the value of realistic live-fire exercises in validating weapons, training crews and assessing the performance of integrated naval capabilities.For the Hellenic Navy, the event provided an opportunity to demonstrate its newly installed missile systems under operational conditions while showcasing coordination between surface combatants and submarine forces.

title: World’s first: China to build 74,000-ton floating research 'island'
content: China has awarded a $413 million contract to build a self-propelled floating research platform designed to support long-term deep-sea scientific research in challenging ocean conditions. The vessel, described as the world’s first floating artificial island dedicated to this type of research, will combine onboard laboratories with a mobile structure intended to remain at sea for extended periods.Shanghai Jiao Tong University will operate the platform, while Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), will handle its design and construction. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028, with delivery planned for June 2030.Unlike a conventional research ship, the proposed platform will use a twin-hull catamaran configuration with a semi-submersible main structure. It is designed to move between research areas while providing accommodation and laboratory space for scientists studying marine ecosystems, ocean engineering and severe weather conditions.Mobile platform designed for rough seasThe planned research vessel will measure approximately 453 feet long and 279 feet wide, with a main deck height of 148 feet. Its displacement is expected to reach 74,000 tons, and it will have a maximum speed of 11 knots, Chinese media reported.The catamaran design is intended to provide stability and seakeeping capabilities during extended operations offshore. According to the project specifications, the platform is designed to operate in Sea State 7, which corresponds to significant wave heights of approximately 20 to 30 feet, and withstand a Category 17 typhoon, with maximum sustained winds exceeding 165 mph.The vessel’s ability to move under its own power is a key part of the concept. Rather than remaining permanently anchored at a single location, it is intended to reposition as research requirements change, combining the mobility of a ship with the working space and long-duration accommodation of a floating facility.Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding says the project will draw on its experience constructing large and technically complex offshore structures, including a sixth-generation semi-submersible drilling platform designed for operations in water depths of up to 9,843 feet.Six laboratories for marine science and engineeringThe floating platform will include six shipborne laboratories focused on marine heavy equipment and systems technology, alongside facilities for studying marine disasters, meteorology and long-term changes in ocean ecosystems.Its research mission is expected to cover both the engineering challenges of working in deep water and the environmental processes affecting the oceans. Long-duration observations can help researchers study changes that are difficult to capture during short research cruises, while onboard engineering facilities could support testing of marine equipment and systems.The vessel is designed to accommodate 238 people, including crew members and researchers. That capacity is intended to support extended missions without requiring the platform to return to port frequently for personnel changes or logistical support.The combination of laboratories, accommodation and a large working platform could also enable researchers to conduct several types of studies from a single location. Its planned delivery in June 2030 leaves several years for detailed design and construction before the platform can begin operations.

title: Five 600 MW hydrogen-ready power ships set for major yard conversion
content: A fleet of high-capacity floating power stations is heading to Singapore for a major engineering refit. Under a new deal, marine engineering firm Seatrium will convert and assemble five next-generation “Whale Class” vessels for Turkey-based operator Karpowership. The ships act as mobile power plants, built to supply electricity directly into national grids from coastal waters.Work on the engineering designs has already begun. The first hull is scheduled to berth at Seatrium’s Tuas Boulevard Yard in December 2027, where technicians will install power hardware, complete mechanical systems, and run pre-commissioning tests.Floating plants are increasingly used to bypass the long construction timelines of onshore power stations. Karpowership builds its vessels with a plug-and-play architecture, allowing them to hook into coastal substations and start generating electricity within 30 days of arrival.The Whale Class represents the operator’s largest design so far. Each vessel is engineered to deploy up to 600 megawatts of electricity. To put that in perspective, a single ship produces enough energy to power hundreds of thousands of homes.Expansion of a working partnershipThe design also addresses the shift toward cleaner fuels. The vessels carry multi-fuel generation machinery designed to run on conventional marine fuels, natural gas, or hydrogen blends without requiring structural rebuilding. High-efficiency layouts ensure fuel moves continuously through the generation train while onboard substations handle step-up transformation for direct transmission ashore.The agreement expands a working partnership between the two companies that began in 2018. Over that period, Seatrium has delivered seven floating storage and regasification units (FSRUs) to Karpowership, with work on two more vessels already secured.This latest project converts earlier plans into firm contracts. In August 2025, both parties signed a letter of intent covering three gas-storage conversions and the integration of up to six new power vessels. The current five-ship deal represents the primary execution phase of that agreement.Global energy outlookExecutives from both firms stressed the project’s engineering demands. Alvin Gan, executive vice president of repairs and upgrades at Seatrium, said the contract marks the yard’s first conversion of the Whale Class series. He noted that the yard’s offshore engineering teams will manage the complex equipment integration needed to secure floating power supplies globally.Gokhan Kocak, chief technical operations officer at Karpowership, added that the new class reflects the company’s shift toward larger, cleaner energy assets. He said Seatrium’s past performance on complex vessel conversions made it the natural partner to deliver the flagship hulls.“Karpowership has transformed global power generation with its innovative Powership model, delivering fast-track and dependable electricity solutions to millions worldwide,” concluded Kocak.“The next-generation Whale Class Powerships demonstrate our continued commitment to innovation, operational excellence and energy security.”The project signals continued demand for rapid-deployment energy infrastructure. As emerging economies and coastal hubs face growing power shortfalls, modular floating plants offer a way to secure grid capacity while keeping the door open to future hydrogen adoption.

title: Chinese carrier and US strike group overlap in western Pacific waters
content: China’s aircraft carrier Liaoning and its accompanying warships are sailing through waters south of the Philippines, potentially setting up an overlap with US and allied naval forces conducting the Keen Sword military exercise in the Philippine Sea. The Chinese carrier group moved beyond the first island chain during a deployment that began on October 14, while the US Navy’s USS Theodore Roosevelt was operating in the region alongside Japanese, Australian, Canadian and French warships.The timing brings two separate military activities into the same strategically important stretch of the western Pacific, although there is no confirmation that the Chinese formation is deliberately heading toward the exercise or that the two carrier groups will come into direct contact. Keen Sword runs from October 19 to 29, with activities taking place across Japan and surrounding waters.Liaoning’s route takes it around the PhilippinesThe four-ship Chinese formation includes the Liaoning and three guided-missile destroyers: the Type 055 vessels Wuxi and Anshan, and the Type 052D destroyer Huainan. Philippine naval vessels reportedly shadowed the group as it sailed near the country’s southwestern coast.Japan’s defense ministry reported that the Chinese warships passed through the Miyako Strait on October 14 to enter the Pacific, then turned toward the South China Sea the following day before heading toward the southern Philippines. The route suggests the group is moving anticlockwise around the Philippine archipelago, reversing the course it took during exercises in October 2024, the South China Morning Post reported. The deployment is Liaoning’s second round of drills in the western Pacific this year. The carrier group is expected to remain deployed for several weeks, overlapping with the Keen Sword drillJapanese authorities also detected Chinese aerial surveillance assets operating near the carrier earlier in the month, including a Y-9 electronic reconnaissance aircraft and a WZ-7 high-altitude unmanned aircraft. However, it remains unclear whether either aircraft continued south with the carrier group.Two carrier operations in a strategically important regionThe USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, was operating in the Philippine Sea with allied warships as part of Keen Sword, according to the US Navy’s 7th Fleet. The first island chain, which stretches from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines, is a central geographic feature in US and Chinese military planning. Chinese forces operating beyond it can train in the wider Pacific, while US and allied forces use regional exercises to practice coordination across maritime and air operations.A potential overlap between the Liaoning group and the multinational force would place the two naval activities in the same broad operating area. But it would not, by itself, indicate a confrontation or establish that Beijing intends to disrupt the exercise.Tensions have also surfaced during earlier carrier deployments. In a report aired by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Beijing said Japanese ships and aircraft repeatedly shadowed the Liaoning group during far-sea training in June. The report said the Type 054B frigate Luohe warned off Japanese vessels, while J-15 fighters operating from the carrier intercepted Japanese P-3C maritime patrol aircraft.

title: Underground carbon storage hits record high as US leads global charge
content: Global geological carbon dioxide (CO₂) storage hit a record 48.1 million US tons (43.6 million metric tons) in 2024, according to a new report by researchers at the Imperial College London.The 2026 Annual Report from the London Register of Subsurface CO₂ Storage covered 70 projects across 17 countries on six continents, providing one of the most comprehensive records of global geological CO₂ storage.The report also added that 464.8 million US tons of CO₂ have been stored underground since 1996. “Our latest report shows that geological CO₂ storage has become a global enterprise, with annual reported storage more than doubling between 2016 and 2024,” Samuel Krevor, director of the Register at Imperial College London, told Phys.org.“The consistency of these operations, and the fact that new countries and projects continue to join the Register, shows that geological storage is demonstrated as a large-scale mitigation technology.”US and Brazil lead global CO₂ storageGeological carbon storage involves capturing CO₂ from industrial operations, power generation, or the atmosphere and injecting it into underground rock formations, where it can remain trapped for thousands of years.According to the London Register of Subsurface CO₂ Storage, annual storage increased from 23.1 million US tons in 2016 to 48.1 million US tons in 2024.The United States reported the most projects in 2024, with 23 projects collectively storing 22.3 million US tons of CO₂.However, Brazil’s Petrobras Santos Basin Pre-Salt Oil Field was the world’s largest individual project globally, reporting 15.7 million US tons, approximately one-third of the global total.China reported 1.9 million US tons in 2024, with contributions from the Shengli Oilfield and the newly included Daqing Aonan Oilfield. Australia contributed 1.9 million US tons. New Zealand and Italy entered the register for the first time.“Where the sources of CO₂ today are dominated by industrial capture, removals from the atmosphere are projected to emerge as the leading technology using geological storage by mid-century,” added Krevor. Research calls for expanded underground CO₂ storage Figures from 2025 show 39.9 million US tons of reported storage from 29 projects across 12 countries. However, the researchers added the data was incomplete.Brazil’s Petrobras Santos Basin project reported 21.6 million US tons for 2025, compared to 15.7 million in 2024.The researchers emphasized that expanding underground CO₂ storage will be essential to meet international climate goals. To meet the 1.5°C (or 2.7°F as a temperature increase) target set out in the Paris Agreement, geological storage must scale to 1.1 billion US tons of CO₂ storage or more per year by 2050.The report also revised previously published storage figures. Cumulative storage through 2023 fell from 387.4 million to 377.0 million US tons, a 2.7 percent reduction.The annual figure for 2023 was also revised downward from 49.8 million to 46.0 million US tons.“These revisions reflect the latest evidence, and we have been explicit in the report about where the accounting for reported storage remains uncertain,” said Dr. Xiaowei Gao, executive director of the Register at Imperial College London.“That transparency matters if geological CO₂ storage is to earn the confidence of policymakers and investors.”

title: 7 Lockheed Martin developments advancing US and allied defense
content: Autonomous aircraft, drone-killing microwaves, and cheaper missile interceptors featured among Lockheed Martin’s major announcements in the third quarter of 2026. The developments span air combat, hypersonic weapons, and the satellite infrastructure that military forces rely on for navigation.In an October 22 roundup, the company highlighted projects intended to strengthen US and allied capabilities while accelerating production and reducing costs. Some involve new systems still under development, while others expand existing programs.Here are seven developments from the roundup and what each is intended to deliver.1. Vectis autonomous aircraft moves toward its first flightLockheed Martin’s Skunk Works is expanding production of Vectis with four additional aircraft as the autonomous platform advances toward a planned first flight in 2027.Building more vehicles will support the program’s development, although the announcement does not establish that the aircraft has completed flight testing or entered operational service.The company describes Vectis as a survivable and adaptable aircraft for future combat requirements. Its development also reflects an effort to use advanced design and manufacturing methods to shorten the path from an initial concept to a flying platform.The first flight will be a milestone in establishing how the design performs beyond the development environment.2. MORFIUS X-Rotor takes microwave defense into the airLockheed MartinMORFIUS X-Rotor is an airborne counter-drone system designed to neutralize more than 50 drones during a single flight, according to Lockheed Martin.Instead of relying on a separate missile for every target, the reusable system carries high-power microwave technology intended to disrupt drone electronics. This gives it a potential role against swarms that could overwhelm defenses through sheer numbers.The company presents the platform as a scalable approach to countering increasingly sophisticated unmanned aircraft.However, the figure describes its intended capability. The roundup does not provide detailed test conditions or establish that the system has achieved the same result against every type of drone swarm.3. Modular payloads could expand hypersonic missionsLockheed MartinLockheed Martin is investing millions of dollars in a Modular Payload Delivery System intended to turn existing hypersonic technologies into a more flexible family of systems.The approach centers on integrating different payloads without repeating the full development process for each configuration. If successful, this could reduce the time and expense of adapting hypersonic technology to different mission requirements.Modularity matters because the usefulness of a high-speed platform depends partly on what it can carry and deliver.The announcement describes a development investment, with faster integration and lower costs presented as intended benefits rather than completed results.4. Germany’s first F-35A reaches rolloutGermany’s first F-35A Lightning II was presented in September, marking a manufacturing milestone in the country’s introduction of the aircraft.The program is intended to strengthen Germany’s air combat capabilities and improve its ability to operate alongside other NATO forces using the F-35.Operating a common aircraft can support closer cooperation across training, maintenance, and missions. However, a rollout ceremony is one stage in a longer process that also includes acceptance, training, and operational preparation.The milestone therefore signals progress toward introducing the aircraft rather than confirming that Germany’s F-35 fleet is already ready for combat.5. AIM-260 agreement targets faster missile productionLockheed MartinLockheed Martin signed a framework agreement with the US Department of War to accelerate production and delivery of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.The company says the weapon is designed to provide greater range and effectiveness against current and emerging threats.The announcement focuses on production, highlighting the importance of delivering advanced weapons in sufficient quantities alongside developing their capabilities.However, the roundup does not disclose production targets, delivery schedules, or detailed missile performance figures. It establishes an agreement to accelerate the program without providing enough information to quantify the resulting increase.6. GPS ground systems receive further modernization fundingLockheed Martin secured an additional $114 million in US Space Force contracts to modernize the GPS ground segment.Although GPS is commonly associated with satellites, its operation also depends on infrastructure on Earth. Ground systems support the constellation and help sustain the positioning, navigation, and timing services used by military forces.The modernization work is intended to improve resilience and reliability.This makes the investment relevant well beyond navigation alone. Dependable timing and positioning underpin a broad range of military activities, making ground infrastructure an essential part of the wider system.7. PAC-3 ACE aims to lower interception costsLockheed MartinLockheed Martin introduced the PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector, or PAC-3 ACE, as a lower-cost interceptor for a range of air and missile threats.According to the company, its intended unit cost is less than half that of the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptor.Built on existing PAC-3 technology, ACE is designed for rapid fielding, with American and European partnerships supporting the effort.Its proposed cost advantage addresses a practical challenge: maintaining enough interceptors to respond to repeated attacks. The roundup, however, does not establish an operational deployment date.Together, these developments show an emphasis on expanding capability while improving affordability and production capacity. Their eventual impact will depend on flight tests, integration, manufacturing progress, and delivery to operational forces.

title: Scientists Uncover a Hidden Secret That Could Transform Chemical Manufacturing
content:
Chemistry
Conceptual image illustrating the electrosynthesis of ε-caprolactone through local pH control. Credit: © Seoul National University College of Engineering
A hidden variable in chemical reactions could hold the key to cleaner and more efficient manufacturing.
Scientists have identified a hidden factor that can determine whether a chemical reaction succeeds or fails. By controlling tiny changes in acidity near electrodes, researchers dramatically improved the production of valuable chemical ingredients, raising the proportion of the desired product from approximately 16% to 97%.
The breakthrough, led by Professor Jaeyune Ryu of the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at Seoul National University College of Engineering, could help make chemical manufacturing safer, cleaner, and more efficient. The researchers developed a method that uses oxygen and electricity to produce compounds used in plastics, medicines, adhesives, and other everyday materials without requiring the separate addition of peroxide oxidants.
Their discovery centers on a surprisingly overlooked factor called “local pH,” which describes the acidity or alkalinity in the immediate surroundings of an electrode. By redesigning a chemical reactor to control the distance between electrodes and the movement of liquid through the system, the team found a way to manage these conditions and greatly improve the reaction’s performance.
The work focused on two important families of chemicals: lactones and epoxides. Lactones are essential starting materials for biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes, while epoxides are used to manufacture adhesives, protective coatings, and epoxy resins found in electronic materials. Both also play important roles in producing pharmaceuticals and other specialized chemicals.
The findings were published in the Journal of the
American Chemical Society (JACS)
, a leading chemistry journal published by the American Chemical Society (ACS).
Conceptual diagram comparing conditions with large local pH deviations near the electrodes (left) and conditions in which those deviations are mitigated (right). Controlling local pH maintains the supply of reactive oxygen species and reduces product degradation, thereby improving reaction efficiency and selectivity. (Bottom) Reactor design incorporating narrow electrode spacing and electrolyte flow, illustrating how increasing the flow rate reduces local pH deviations near the electrodes. Credit: © Journal of the American Chemical Society, originally published in Journal of the American Chemical Society
The Hidden Chemistry That Can Make or Break a Reaction
The research builds on a technique known as organic electrosynthesis, which uses electrical energy to drive reactions that produce carbon-based chemical compounds.
This approach has attracted growing interest because it may reduce the need for some of the chemical oxidizing and reducing agents commonly used in traditional manufacturing. Such agents help reactions proceed by accepting or donating electrons, but some can be hazardous to handle and generate unwanted waste.
Until now, much of the effort to improve organic electrosynthesis has centered on familiar factors, including the electrical voltage, the materials used for electrodes, and the composition of the liquid in which reactions occur.
However, the researchers suspected that something important was being overlooked: the microscopic chemical environment directly next to each electrode.
This is where molecules exchange electrons and undergo chemical transformations. Although the surrounding solution may appear uniform, conditions within this tiny region can be dramatically different.
One particularly important factor is pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline a substance is.
During an electrochemical reaction, hydrogen ions, also known as protons, can be produced or consumed at the electrodes. If these ions are generated or removed faster than they can move through the liquid, the pH near the electrode may become very different from the pH measured in the rest of the solution.
The researchers found that these local differences can influence several critical parts of a reaction. They can change how reactive oxygen species are produced, alter the behavior of the starting molecules, and even affect whether the finished products remain stable or begin to break down.
In other words, a reaction can fail even when the overall solution appears to have the right chemical conditions.
An Overlooked Problem May Affect Many Chemical Reactions
To determine whether this phenomenon might extend beyond their own experiments, the researchers examined more than 600 scientific papers on organic electrosynthesis published since 2010.
They found that approximately 89% of the studies involved reactions at one or more electrodes in which both electrons and protons were transferred.
This matters because the movement of protons can change local acidity. The finding suggests that overlooked pH differences near electrodes could influence a wide range of electrochemical reactions, rather than just a few specialized examples.
The team also measured how extreme these differences could become.
Even when the overall solution was essentially neutral, the researchers estimated that conditions near the cathode, the electrode where reduction occurs, could reach approximately pH 11, making the area strongly alkaline.
Meanwhile, the region around the anode, where oxidation takes place, could reach approximately pH 2.5, creating a strongly acidic environment.
These changes can have major consequences. Under such conditions, the reactive oxygen species needed to drive a reaction may become less available. Starting materials can change chemical form, and newly formed products may break down more rapidly.
Simply adjusting the acidity of the entire solution therefore may not solve the problem. What matters is the environment directly around the electrodes, where the chemistry actually happens.
Making Valuable Chemicals With Oxygen and Electricity
To demonstrate their discovery, the scientists investigated a well-established chemical process called Baeyer–Villiger oxidation.
This reaction adds an oxygen atom to a type of organic molecule known as a ketone, converting it into an ester or lactone. Lactones are ring-shaped compounds that serve as important building blocks for materials such as biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes.
Traditionally, Baeyer–Villiger oxidation often requires highly reactive oxidizing chemicals, including peroxyacids. Although effective, these substances can create difficulties involving safe handling, chemical waste, and the treatment of unwanted byproducts.
The Seoul National University team developed a different approach.
Instead of supplying these oxidants from outside the system, the researchers used electricity to activate oxygen gas at an electrode. This produced reactive oxygen species capable of transferring oxygen atoms into organic molecules.
To establish where the oxygen in the final products came from, the team conducted isotope-tracing experiments. These tests confirmed that the incorporated oxygen originated from oxygen gas rather than water.
The scientists also discovered that the two electrodes could work together in an important way.
At the cathode, oxygen reduction generates reactive oxygen species that initiate the oxygen-transfer reaction. Hydrogen peroxide formed during this process can then be converted back into reactive oxygen species at the anode.
This cooperation helps sustain the supply of reactive chemical species necessary for the reaction.
However, the entire process depends heavily on the acidity near the electrodes. If local pH becomes too extreme, the chemistry can become much less effective.
A Simple Reactor Redesign Boosts Selectivity From 16% to 97%
Once the researchers understood the importance of local pH, they investigated how to control it.
Using computer simulations and electrochemical measurements, they developed a reactor design that places the electrodes closer together while allowing the electrolyte, the electrically conductive liquid carrying the reaction ingredients, to flow between them.
The idea was to prevent extreme acidity differences from developing.
Because the area near the anode tends to become acidic while the area near the cathode becomes alkaline, bringing these regions closer together and circulating the liquid helps counterbalance their effects.
The results were striking.
Under conditions where local pH differences were not effectively controlled, approximately 16% of the relevant products formed were the desired target compound. With the improved reactor design, that selectivity rose to approximately 97%.
This increase in selectivity means the reaction became much better at producing the intended substance rather than unwanted products.
The researchers also discovered that changing the flow of the electrolyte had a powerful effect on production.
Across the flow rates they tested, the amount of product generated per unit time increased by approximately 14 times from the lowest to the highest flow rate.
Moving the electrodes closer together also made a difference. When the distance between them was reduced from 20 mm to 4 mm, the production rate increased by approximately 2.2 times.
Perhaps most revealing was what happened when the liquid was not allowed to flow.
Even though the applied voltage and the solution’s composition remained unchanged, the researchers obtained almost none of the desired product.
This showed just how important the immediate chemical environment can be. The success of an electrochemical reaction depends on more than the ingredients, voltage, and electrode materials. The physical design of the reactor and the microscopic conditions it creates can be equally critical.
Applications for Biodegradable Plastics, Medicines, and Electronics
The researchers then explored whether their approach could be used to manufacture different kinds of useful chemicals.
Using their optimized conditions, they successfully synthesized lactones from 18 different ketone compounds.
One important example was ε-caprolactone, which they produced with an 82% yield.
This compound is a starting material for polycaprolactone, a biodegradable polymer used in medical applications such as surgical sutures and drug-delivery systems.
The researchers also applied their local pH control strategy to the production of epoxides, successfully obtaining products from six different alkene starting materials.
Epoxides are important ingredients in adhesives, surface coatings, and epoxy resins used in electronics. They are also valuable intermediates in the production of pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals.
Together, these experiments showed that controlling the microscopic environment around electrodes could have applications beyond a single reaction.
The findings suggest a potentially versatile way to improve the production of many commercially important chemical ingredients.
Toward Cleaner and More Sustainable Chemical Manufacturing
One of the most promising aspects of the technique is that it uses oxygen and electricity while reducing the need for externally added peroxide oxidants.
The reactions also take place at room temperature and normal atmospheric pressure, avoiding the need for separate equipment to heat or pressurize the system.
These characteristics could make certain chemical processes simpler and potentially safer.
Because electricity provides the energy needed to drive the reactions, the approach could eventually be combined with renewable energy sources to support more sustainable chemical manufacturing.
The researchers believe that pharmaceutical ingredients and other high-value specialty chemicals could be particularly promising applications.
These products often require careful control of reaction conditions and strict safety measures. Electrochemical methods may offer advantages by limiting the need to handle hazardous oxidizing agents and potentially allowing production in relatively compact equipment.
However, the technology is not yet ready for widespread industrial use. Further optimization and testing at larger production scales will be needed to determine whether the laboratory results can be reproduced economically and reliably in commercial manufacturing.
A New Way to Think About Chemical Reactions
Beyond its immediate applications, the discovery offers a different perspective on how electrochemical reactions should be designed.
Traditionally, researchers have concentrated on choosing the right starting materials, catalysts, electrode surfaces, voltages, and solution compositions.
The Seoul National University team’s findings indicate that controlling the tiny environment where molecules actually react may be just as important.
This shifts attention toward “designing the environment in which molecules actually react.”
Professor Jaeyune Ryu, who supervised the research, said, “This study transforms ‘local pH’ near the electrode from a hidden variable into a controllable design principle.”
He added, “To improve the efficiency of organic electrosynthesis, we need to design not only the reaction substrates and catalysts, but also the environment in which the molecules actually react.”
The researchers believe this principle could reveal opportunities to improve other electrochemical processes, particularly those involving the movement of both electrons and protons.
Rather than treating local acidity as an unavoidable side effect, future chemical reactors could be deliberately engineered to maintain conditions that favor the desired reactions.
Reference: “Local pH Control Promotes Oxygen-Atom Transfer Electrosynthesis” by Seonghyeon Min, Junghoon Lee, Hanju Kim and Jaeyune Ryu, 4 September 2026,
Journal of the American Chemical Society
DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c12994
The study’s co-first authors were Seonghyeon Min and Junghoon Lee, both M.S. students in Seoul National University’s Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering. Hanju Kim, an integrated M.S./Ph.D. student, participated as a co-author, with Professor Ryu overseeing the research.
Min and Lee plan to continue investigating how local reaction environments influence organic electrosynthesis, with the goal of extending the approach to a broader range of chemical reactions and manufacturing processes.
The research was supported by Seoul National University, the National Research Foundation of Korea, and the Institute for Basic Science (IBS).
