title: NASA’s Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Radiation Mystery Near the Moon
content:
A lithium fluoride crystal exposed to blue light, showing recorded tracks of ionizing particles under a fluorescence microscope. Credit: IFJ PAN
Radiation near the Moon can pass straight through the body, yet preliminary Artemis I measurements suggest a smaller-than-expected increase in exposure compared with low Earth orbit.
Beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field, astronauts face a constant bombardment of high-energy particles from deep space. But how much radiation would they actually absorb during a journey around the Moon? NASA’s Artemis I mission offered a rare opportunity to find out. Aboard the uncrewed Orion spacecraft, two human-shaped mannequins carried more than 10,000 tiny crystal detectors that recorded radiation exposure throughout their simulated bodies.
Surprisingly, radiation doses near the Moon were only moderately higher than those in low Earth orbit, a smaller increase than researchers might have expected.
Among these detectors were experimental lithium fluoride crystals developed by physicists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. Flown as part of the Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment (MARE), the crystals captured microscopic traces of cosmic radiation during Orion’s journey in late November and early December 2022. A new study published in
Radiation Measurements
explains how scientists decoded those traces, revealing new details about radiation exposure in deep space and demonstrating a promising technique for detecting particles that conventional instruments can overlook.
Tracks of cosmic radiation particles recorded in lithium fluoride crystal detectors during the Artemis I lunar flyby mission. Credit: IFJ PAN
Higher doses without Earth’s radiation belts
“Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet’s magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect,” says Prof. Pawel Bilski of IFJ PAN, a co-author of the paper.
Inside the Artemis I mannequins, known as human phantoms, the recorded radiation dose was essentially uniform. Galactic radiation is more prominent near the Moon, and its particles have such high energies that they can pass through an entire body, depositing only part of their energy along the way. That pattern differed from measurements made during the MATROSHKA experiment aboard the International Space Station more than a decade earlier. There, low-energy protons from Earth’s Van Allen belts contributed part of the dose and lost their energy at different depths inside the phantoms, producing an uneven distribution of radiation exposure.
Blue light reveals radiation’s tracks
Both MARE phantoms carried the experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors, some highly enriched in the isotope lithium-7. The Cracow team also supplied nearly 600 crystalline detectors of another type, known as thermoluminescent detectors.
Cross-sections of the phantoms used in the Artemis I mission, showing the locations where radiation detectors were mounted. Credit: DLR
“The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope,” explains Prof. Bilski.
As particles of ionizing radiation pass through lithium fluoride, they create defects in its crystal lattice, the orderly arrangement of atoms within the material. These defects act as color centers. During laboratory readout, blue light excites the centers, making them emit red fluorescence that can be observed under a microscope. Conventional plastic track detectors require chemical etching before their tracks can be read, but lithium fluoride needs no such treatment. A standard fluorescence microscope allowed the researchers to examine the tracks from the lunar mission quickly and without difficulty.
Radiation tracks conventional detectors miss
Extracting quantitative measurements required more complex calibration methods because cosmic radiation bears little resemblance to a controlled laboratory beam. Typical physics experiments expose detectors to particles of the same type, with well-defined energies and a precisely known direction of arrival. Cosmic radiation contains all naturally occurring types of particles and atomic nuclei, spanning a very broad energy range and arriving from every direction.
Phantoms equipped with radiation detectors, installed inside the Orion capsule during the Artemis I lunar mission. Credit: NASA
With tracks running through the crystals at different angles, the microscope brings a segment approximately one micrometer in size into focus, while its camera also captures a blurred glow from the remaining portions. That extra light affects fluorescence intensity, the primary measurement used to assess ionization density, or how densely a particle knocks electrons out of atoms along its path. Track shape also matters. Highly ionizing particles leave continuous, clearly defined lines, while weakly ionizing particles can leave a series of separate dots, further affecting the measured intensity.
“After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date,” Prof. Bilski emphasizes.
IFJ PAN developed its fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors a decade ago and has continuously improved them since. The crystals used on Artemis I were grown using the Czochralski method, in which a crystal is pulled from molten material. Their dimensions are measured in millimeters rather than centimeters, making them convenient for people to wear. They also resolve tracks more finely than conventional chemically etched plastic detectors, allowing higher radiation doses to be recorded while individual tracks remain distinguishable. Their broad range of detectable particle types and energies enables a better assessment of total radiation exposure.
Lithium fluoride detectors can also record neutron doses, particularly when enriched in lithium-6. Neutrons react with lithium nuclei inside the material, producing secondary charged particles locally. Those particles then interact with the crystal much as incoming ionizing radiation does, leaving a detectable record.
Reference: “Application of LiF fluorescent nuclear track detectors for measurements of cosmic radiation at the lunar orbit within the MARE experiment” by P. Bilski, A. Kilian, M. Sankowska, T. Horwacik and T. Berger, 1 September 2026,
Radiation Measurements
DOI: 10.1016/j.radmeas.2026.107806
The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

title: A Solar Storm Heading Toward Earth Suddenly Changed in Ways Scientists Didn’t Predict
content:
A coronal mass ejection (CME) erupts from the Sun, releasing a massive cloud of magnetized plasma into space. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered surprising behavior inside a powerful solar eruption that challenges existing models and could change how researchers predict space weather.
A massive eruption on the Sun sent a cloud of magnetized plasma racing toward Earth, where it underwent an extraordinary transformation. Over a distance of just 13 million miles, the cloud expanded by 21% as the plasma inside became three times hotter, defying expectations about how these solar structures evolve.
Researchers led by the University of Iowa documented the rapid growth using observations from two spacecraft positioned along the cloud’s path. Their findings challenge existing models of solar storms and could improve predictions of space weather events capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, and electrical grids.
A Rare Alignment Captures a Changing Solar Cloud
The cloud originated from a coronal mass ejection on November 4 and 5, 2021. These powerful solar eruptions release enormous quantities of hot, electrically charged gas threaded with magnetic fields. Some form magnetic clouds containing twisted bundles of magnetic field lines that travel through interplanetary space.
As the crescent-shaped cloud approached Earth, the Solar Orbiter spacecraft recorded its structure approximately 78 million miles from the Sun. The Wind spacecraft later measured the same cloud about 91 million miles from the Sun. Both spacecraft happened to lie along nearly the same line, allowing scientists to compare the cloud’s properties at two relatively close points in its journey. The eruption also produced a major geomagnetic storm on Earth.
“First, it’s rare these two spacecraft would be aligned on a Sun-Earth axis,” says Shirsh Soni, a postdoctoral research fellow in physics and astronomy at the University of Iowa. “Then, second, for them to be aligned like that during an interplanetary coronal mass ejection is so much rarer.”
A physics team led by the University of Iowa has described a “super expanded” magnetic cloud created by a coronal mass ejection on the Sun. The cloud’s dimensions were captured in two intervals of relatively short time and distance by two spacecraft, Solar Orbiter and Wind. Those observations led to findings that the crescent-shaped cloud grew by a fifth of its size as it approached Earth. Credit: David Miles lab, University of Iowa
Solar Wind Triggers Unexpectedly Rapid Expansion
The measurements showed that the magnetic cloud expanded at approximately 192 kilometers per second (119 miles per second), substantially faster than the typical range of 50 to 100 kilometers per second (31 to 62 miles per second). The researchers called this unusually rapid growth a “super expansion.”
The process began when the cloud encountered the surrounding solar wind, a continuous stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun at speeds that can reach approximately 1 million mph. The interaction initially compressed the cloud, but its internal plasma subsequently heated to three times its earlier temperature, driving the dramatic expansion.
“In a typical interplanetary coronal mass ejection, when it encounters the solar wind, it could decelerate or accelerate,” Soni explains. “In this case, it expanded a lot.”
Findings Challenge Existing Solar Storm Models
The team also discovered that the cloud’s magnetic field pressure remained unchanged despite its substantial growth. This behavior differed from predictions produced by existing models, suggesting that magnetic clouds may undergo more complex changes during their journeys through the solar system than previously recognized.
Because the two spacecraft observed the same cloud along its path, the researchers could directly track changes that would have been difficult to distinguish using a single observation point. Such measurements are particularly valuable for understanding how coronal mass ejections develop before reaching Earth, where their magnetic fields can interact with Earth’s magnetosphere and trigger geomagnetic disturbances.
“We have assumed that magnetic clouds from interplanetary coronal mass ejections will evolve in the same way,” says Soni, the study’s corresponding author. “In this study, we show the magnetic cloud can expand dramatically in a short period of time and space, which could have impacts to Earth that we wouldn’t have known about.”
Reference: “Superexpansion of interplanetary coronal mass ejection observed by Solar Orbiter and Wind spacecraft within 0.14 au radial separation” by Shirsh Lata Soni, Ankush Bhaskar, R Selva Kumaran and David Miles, 24 April 2026,
Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag350
Soni’s research was funded through a previous fellowship provided by the University of Michigan.

title: Why Do Some People Get Fevers After Vaccines? Scientists May Have Found the Answer
content:
Gut microbes may help shape how strongly the body responds to vaccination. Flagellins produced by motile gut bacteria can promote inflammation and contribute to differences in fever responses after vaccination. Credit: MPI f. Biology Tübingen / 99Designs (AI generated)
The microbes in your gut may help explain why you develop a fever after a vaccine while someone else feels fine.
Two people can receive the same vaccine and have very different experiences. One develops a fever and feels miserable for a day, while the other barely notices anything. Scientists have long sought to understand why these reactions vary so widely, and new research suggests that part of the answer may lie in the trillions of microbes living in our intestines.
An international research team found that people who developed stronger fevers after vaccination already showed signs of heightened inflammation and distinctive gut microbial activity before receiving their shots. When researchers transferred their gut microbes into mice, the animals also developed stronger inflammatory responses to vaccination. The findings point to a bacterial protein called flagellin as a possible contributor and raise intriguing questions about whether diet could influence how the body responds to vaccines.
Before The Shot, Different Starting Points
Vaccination prevents infectious diseases and protects public health, but concerns about fever and flu-like symptoms can discourage people from getting vaccinated. Understanding why these reactions vary could help researchers find ways to reduce them and address a source of vaccine hesitancy.
The gut microbiome is a plausible place to look because its trillions of microorganisms continually communicate with the immune system, helping shape its baseline activity. Because microbial communities differ between people, the same vaccine may encounter very different immune starting points.
To investigate, researchers led by Ruth Ley at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen established the µHEAT (Microbial-Human Ecology and Temperature) study. With support from Meral Esen at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Tübingen, they recruited healthy young adults receiving a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine in 2021 and 2022.
Participants provided fecal samples for microbial analysis and blood samples for immune measurements. They also regularly recorded their temperature during the week before and the week after vaccination.
A Bacterial Signal Linked to Fever
Organizing the study during the pandemic required the team to recruit participants before they had already received their vaccines, while keeping visits and measurements manageable.
“It was a challenging time to set up a new human study, with the pandemic ongoing,” says lead author Kelsey Huus, who led µHEAT during her postdoctoral research and is now an assistant professor at the University of Ottawa in Canada. “We didn’t want to burden participants with too many measurements or visits, and it was a bit of a race against time to get the study organized before everyone was already vaccinated. But it was absolutely worth it, because the project yielded some very exciting results.”
Some participants developed substantial fevers. Before vaccination, their gut microbes showed greater activity in genes involved in bacterial movement, particularly those used to make whip-like swimming structures called flagella.
Flagella are built from proteins called flagellins. Because pathogens such as Salmonella also produce flagellins, the immune system recognizes these proteins as potential danger signals and responds with inflammation. Blood and fecal measurements suggested that participants who developed stronger fevers already had higher levels of inflammation before vaccination.
Testing the Microbiome in Mice
The human observations revealed an association, but the researchers needed an experiment to test whether the microbes themselves could influence vaccine responses. They transferred participants’ fecal microbiomes into mice that lacked intestinal microbes of their own, then vaccinated the animals.
Mice receiving microbes from participants with stronger fever responses developed more severe inflammation than those receiving microbes from people with milder responses. The effect depended partly on the animals’ ability to sense flagellin, providing evidence that the bacterial protein contributed to the response.
“Vaccination provides a controlled way to understand why people can respond so differently to the same immune challenge,” says Ley, director of the Department of Microbiome Science. “Our findings show that microbial flagellin is one contributor to this baseline immune state, providing a potential link between differences in the gut microbiome and differences in immune responses.”
Could Diet Influence The Response?
The team next explored what might encourage gut microbes to produce more flagellin. Participants eating plant-based diets tended to have weaker fever responses, making diet a candidate for further investigation.
“We could see that certain food additives increased flagellin production by gut microbes in vitro,” explains Benoit Chassaing, Inserm research director at Institut Pasteur. “Interestingly, these findings show that components of an industrialized diet may promote the growth of flagellated gut bacteria and increase overall flagellin production.”
Animal experiments offered further evidence. “We found that a high-fat Western-style diet enhanced inflammatory vaccine responses in mice,” says co-author Hirohito Abo of Georgia State University in Atlanta.
“While we could not show that diet determines vaccine responses in humans, our study findings suggest that diet is one factor capable of modifying a pro-inflammatory microbiome,” Huus says. “Interventional studies in people will be needed to determine whether dietary changes can alter microbial flagellin production in humans and, in turn, vaccine responses like fever.”
Beyond Vaccine Side Effects
Future trials could investigate whether interventions targeting the microbiome can reduce strong fevers after vaccination. More broadly, the study suggests that gut microbes help establish an immune state that may influence responses to challenges beyond vaccines.
“Ultimately, this work adds to growing evidence that the gut microbiome plays a central role in human immune health,” Huus adds. “Understanding these interactions could now open new opportunities to improve how we predict, prevent, and manage individual differences in immune responses.”

title: Scientists Discover a Protective Gene That Could Help Keep the Brain Young
content:
Researchers discovered that a little-understood gene can reduce harmful fat accumulation in brain immune cells. Credit: Shutterstock
Boosting a protective gene helped aging mice preserve memory, suggesting that strengthening the brain’s own defenses could offer a way to delay cognitive decline in people.
Some older adults remain cognitively resilient even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers investigating the biological mechanisms behind this resilience have identified a gene called
that may help protect the aging brain from memory loss.
In a study published in
Nature Neuroscience
, researchers found that increasing
activity in aging mice protected against synapse loss, inflammation, and disruptions in fat metabolism. Boosting the gene in middle-aged mice before substantial cognitive decline developed also changed the trajectory of age-related memory loss.
The study’s lead and senior authors are Cinzia Vicidomini, PhD, and Amar Sahay, PhD, respectively, of the Mass General Brigham Department of Psychiatry, the Harvard Stem Cell Institute, and the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT.
Identifying the brain’s natural defenses against aging
As the brain ages, protective and harmful biological processes compete to influence its health. When harmful changes become dominant, synapses deteriorate, inflammation increases, and problems with lipid metabolism can interfere with normal brain function.
Cinzia Vicidomini, PhD. Credit: Mass General Brigham
“As humans age, both protective and harmful biological processes shape brain health. When the balance shifts in favor of harmful processes, age-related changes in the brain can accelerate, including synapse loss, disruptions in lipid metabolism and chronic inflammation,” said Vicidomini.
To identify factors that might counteract these changes, the researchers searched for genes activated in response to synapse loss in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for memory. They focused on dentate granule cells, neurons involved in forming and processing memories.
Their investigation identified
, a gene that produces a secreted enzyme called a phospholipase. Its role in the brain had previously been unknown.
The researchers discovered that
levels increased in the hippocampus during aging and under conditions of brain inflammation. The gene was also expressed at higher levels in older adults whose brains showed signs of Alzheimer’s disease pathology but who remained cognitively resilient.
These findings suggested that
could be part of a natural protective response that helps the brain withstand age-related damage.
Boosting the gene protects memory in aging mice
To investigate the gene’s function, the team used genetic and viral tools to decrease or increase
activity in the brains of aging mice.
Reducing the gene’s activity worsened several features of brain aging, including synapse loss, inflammatory changes in microglia, increased reactivity in astrocytes, and impaired formation and maturation of new neurons. The mice also experienced disruptions in lipid metabolism, accumulation of fat droplets in brain cells, and greater memory impairment.
Increasing
activity had the opposite effect. It protected against many of these changes, helped maintain healthy communication between neurons, and preserved memory.
“Remarkably, boosting
in middle-aged mice before they developed substantial cognitive decline altered the trajectory of age-related memory loss,” said Sahay.
The results suggest that strengthening this protective mechanism before significant damage occurs may be especially valuable.
Reducing harmful fat buildup in brain immune cells
The researchers also uncovered a connection between
and the regulation of fats in the brain.
Microglia, the brain’s immune cells, help clear waste, maintain synapses, and support neurons. During aging and Alzheimer’s disease, however, these cells can accumulate lipid droplets, making them less effective and contributing to chronic inflammation.
Experiments using human microglia derived from induced pluripotent stem cells showed that neuronal PLA2G2F could influence these immune cells. Increasing its activity reduced the accumulation of lipid droplets and cholesterol esters, a form of stored cholesterol. Both are commonly found at elevated levels in microglia associated with Alzheimer’s disease.
Amar Sahay, PhD. Credit: Mass General Brigham
Further experiments showed that disrupting the enzyme’s catalytic site prevented its ability to mobilize lipid droplets and reduce inflammatory changes in brain cells. This suggests that the enzyme’s biochemical activity is important for its protective effects.
Together, the findings point to PLA2G2F as a protective signal released by neurons that helps maintain healthy lipid metabolism and limit inflammation across brain cells.
Could this approach help prevent Alzheimer’s disease?
Aging is the greatest risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease, making the discovery of natural mechanisms that preserve memory particularly important.
The researchers believe that increasing
activity could eventually offer a way to strengthen cognitive resilience and potentially delay the onset of mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease.
“Our findings suggest that increasing
activity during aging could potentially help maintain cognitive resilience and delay or prevent the onset of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease,” said Sahay.
However, the evidence for memory protection currently comes from animal experiments. Although the researchers also demonstrated beneficial effects in human microglia, it remains unknown whether increasing
activity would safely protect memory in people.
“Additional studies will be needed to determine whether this approach can be safely translated into therapies for patients,” Sahay said. “We are actively exploring potential ways to safely increase
levels in the aging brain and in Alzheimer’s disease as a possible therapeutic strategy.”

title: A Simple Diet Change Could Transform Kidney Disease Treatment, 10-Year Study Finds
content:
Kidney disease occurs when the kidneys gradually lose their ability to filter waste, balance fluids, and regulate essential substances in the blood. As the condition progresses, harmful substances can accumulate in the body, increasing the risk of serious complications, including kidney failure. Credit: Shutterstock
For kidney patients with acid buildup, a decade-long trial suggests fruits and vegetables may offer what a standard treatment did not: fewer hospital visits without higher overall costs.
When kidneys lose their ability to function properly, the consequences can extend far beyond waste buildup. People with chronic kidney disease can also develop excess acid in their blood, a condition known as metabolic acidosis that can contribute to worsening kidney function and other serious complications. Doctors commonly treat this imbalance with sodium bicarbonate, but new research suggests that a surprisingly simple dietary approach could offer greater long-term benefits.
In a decade-long clinical trial, researchers found that patients who received fruits and vegetables to help neutralize excess acid experienced substantially fewer hospitalizations and emergency department visits than those receiving usual care. O
ver 10 years, the 36 patients in the dietary group had just 14 hospitalizations and 20 emergency visits, compared with 64 and 88, respectively, among the 36 patients receiving usual care. Only four patients in the dietary group required dialysis, compared with 16 in the usual-care group, raising intriguing questions about the role of nutrition in protecting kidney health.
Two acid treatments, different long-term results
The trial enrolled 108 adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) and metabolic acidosis, the medical term for excess acid buildup in the body. Researchers randomly assigned participants to three groups of 36, receiving fruits and vegetables, oral sodium bicarbonate, or usual care. The dietary approach used base-producing fruits and vegetables, which help counter acidity. Both the dietary treatment and sodium bicarbonate were intended to reduce dietary acid by half, allowing researchers to compare two approaches with the same acid-reduction goal.
Participants were followed annually for 10 years. Across all three groups, researchers recorded 115 hospitalizations and 166 emergency department visits, and 34 patients needed dialysis. Despite sharing the dietary treatment’s acid-reduction goal, sodium bicarbonate showed no difference from usual care in hospitalizations, emergency department visits, or progression to dialysis.
Kidney benefits without higher overall costs
“Treatment of metabolic acidosis with fruits and vegetables was associated with more favorable long-term clinical outcomes and health care utilization than standard treatment with sodium bicarbonate or usual care, without increasing overall health-system or societal costs,” said corresponding author Nimrit Goraya, MD, of Baylor Scott and White Health.
The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, October 22–25. The trial’s comparison of individual treatments also raises the question of how dietary interventions might affect care and spending across a larger population.
“These findings support evaluating dietary interventions in chronic kidney disease not only at the individual-patient level but also at the population level, where the cumulative clinical and economic benefits may be substantial. They also highlight the potential quality-of-life and health-system value of investing in fruits and vegetables as a treatment strategy, particularly when favorable clinical outcomes can be achieved without increasing overall costs.”
Meeting: ASN Kidney Week

title: A Bizarre 170-Million-Year-Old Predator Is Rewriting What We Know About Ancient Crocodiles
content:
An artist’s restoration of Ctenosuchus tenuidens. Credit: Nathan Dehaut
A Moroccan crocodile relative’s teeth resemble those of prehistoric filter feeders, suggesting that different reptile groups independently evolved similar tools for catching tiny aquatic prey.
A crocodile relative that lived around 170 million years ago had a long, narrow snout lined with exceptionally thin, needle-like teeth. No known close relative has teeth quite like them. Their delicacy suggests a diet of very small fish, crustaceans such as fairy shrimp, and other small aquatic creatures rather than large prey.
Scientists at the University of Portsmouth and Hassan II University of Casablanca, Morocco, identified the new species, named
Ctenosuchus tenuidens
. It belonged to the thalattosuchians, a group of marine and freshwater reptiles that lived during the age of the dinosaurs. Its fossils came from rocks formed in ancient rivers and lakes in what is now the Atlas Mountains of southeastern Morocco.
Large prey could break fragile teeth
The researchers examined the fossil teeth under powerful microscopes and studied their internal structure, finding specialized ridges and a closely spaced arrangement. For lead author Hamzah Imran, from the University of Portsmouth’s School of the Environment and Life Sciences, the teeth’s fragility offered a clue to what the animal could safely catch.
The fossil Ctenosuchus tenuidens. Credit: University of Portsmouth
He said: “The teeth are so fine that we don’t think it was catching normal prey. If it caught a big fish, and the fish wriggled, those delicate teeth would get smashed. We think the animal was probably eating soft prey like shrimp, worms and tiny fish, so nothing that would break its teeth.
“These feeding habits make this particular species very different to other long-snouted crocodiles, so it really is quite an exciting discovery!”
Black circles reveal comb-like teeth
Recognizing the teeth in the first place required a microscope and careful work with a scalpel. Imran recalled: “We noticed these little black circles on either side of the long bone in the middle of one of the fossils, so we put it under a microscope.
“We carefully scratched around one of the black circles with a scalpel, and as we uncovered more of it, it became longer and longer. That’s when we realized these little black circles were actually incredibly thin teeth.
“These comb-like teeth inspired the name
Ctenosuchus tenuidens
as ‘cteno’ means ‘comb,’ ‘suchus’ means ‘crocodile,’ and ‘tenuidens’ means ‘thin teeth.’”
Hamzah at his desk with the fossil. Credit: University of Portsmouth
Similar teeth, separate evolutionary paths
Although unusual among its close relatives,
Ctenosuchus
had teeth resembling those of other prehistoric animals. Similar teeth occur in ancient aquatic reptiles called mesosaurs and in certain long-snouted pterosaurs that lived millions of years later. Its jaws and teeth share features with those of the Jurassic pterosaurs
Gnathosaurus
Ctenochasma
, which scientists believe were filter feeders, using their teeth to separate small food items from water. These similarities indicate that different groups independently evolved comparable feeding adaptations.
The Moroccan fossils broaden scientists’ understanding of the habitats and feeding roles occupied by Jurassic crocodile relatives in Gondwana, the southern supercontinent that included modern-day Africa. They also add to the picture of the varied prehistoric ecosystems that once existed in Morocco.
Imran added: “It just shows there is much more out there that needs to be explored. Morocco has an incredibly rich fossil history, but there is still so much waiting to be discovered.”
Reference: “A new teleosauroid (Crocodylomorpha, Thalattosuchia) with a unique dentition from the Middle Jurassic of eastern Morocco” by Hamzah Imran, David M. Martill, Roy E. Smith, Samir Zouhri, James Gunn and Nizar Ibrahim, 8 October 2026,
Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology
DOI: 10.1080/02724634.2026.2728670

title: Medieval Children Were Exposed to Shocking Levels of Lead, 1,000 Years Before the Industrial Revolution
content:
Gold-bound beaver-tooth pendant from the Wigber Low cemetery (mid-7th century). Credit: Sheffield Museums Trust
Children in medieval English mining communities faced lead exposure matching or exceeding that in Industrial Revolution cities, with social standing apparently shaping who bore the greatest burden.
Between the 16th and 19th centuries, lead producers in the Derbyshire Peak District of central England repeatedly remelted waste left by Roman and medieval workings. Reusing that material erased many of the industrial traces archaeologists would normally examine to establish when mining and smelting resumed after Roman Britain. A record survived, however, in the teeth of the people who lived there.
Lead preserved in tooth enamel has now provided the first definitive evidence that production was established by the middle of the seventh century AD. It also reveals the extent of childhood exposure. Even in the seventh century, lead concentrations in the mining communities matched or exceeded those found in people from industrial cities around 1750 to 1850.
A mining history preserved in teeth
Mining and smelting exposed communities to lead through contaminated dust, fumes, and materials. Tooth enamel forms during childhood and does not remodel later in life, preserving a record of the lead absorbed while a person was growing up. Measuring the metal locked within enamel allowed researchers to reconstruct childhood exposure from about 650 to 1500 and compare its extent across individuals and communities.
The Castleton cemeteries: a) Joule Yard; b) Spital Field. Credit: Colin Merrony & Anna Bloxam
The research was led by the University of Nottingham in collaboration with the British Geological Survey, the University of Sheffield, York Archaeology, and Castleton Historical Society. Combining archaeology, history, chemistry, and environmental science, it is the first study to analyze lead contamination in people who mined and smelted the metal in western Europe’s largest medieval lead-producing region.
The samples came from three cemetery populations spanning the industry’s revival and expansion. Wigber Low, in the Derbyshire White Peak, dates to the seventh century. At Castleton, Joule Yard dates from the seventh to 11th centuries, while Spital Field dates from the 12th to 15th centuries. The research builds on decades of archaeological investigation, including earlier work by Colin Merrony at the University of Sheffield, who identified and excavated key medieval burial sites in the region.
To place the measurements in context, the researchers compared these communities with populations elsewhere in Britain, ranging from the Neolithic period through the Industrial Revolution. This comparison revealed how high childhood exposure already was during the early medieval period, long before the industry reached its greatest scale.
Lead author Christopher Loveluck, Professor of Medieval European Archaeology at the University of Nottingham’s Department of Classics and Archaeology, said, “The team is delighted to have finally confirmed definitively the date by which the early medieval lead industry was established in the Peak District, by the mid-7th century AD, through evidence provided by the people themselves, providing the foundations of western Europe’s largest lead-producing region between the late 12th and 16th centuries.”
Medieval pollution peaks around 1200
Peveril Castle at Castleton, next to the Peak Cavern lead mine which overlooks the Joule Yard cemetery (late 7th to 11th century). Credit: Peak District National Park Authority
That timing also connects the people’s teeth with evidence collected far beyond their communities. Previous studies of Alpine ice cores and sediment cores from river channels, lakes, and peat bogs across western Europe identified a rise in atmospheric lead pollution around 1200, attributed especially to British production. The enamel findings provide a direct link between those environmental records and the people living and working in one of Europe’s major lead-producing landscapes.
Higher status, lower lead exposure
Within the mining communities, exposure varied with apparent social standing. People buried with high-status grave goods, including weapons, generally had much lower lead concentrations than those whose burials were less richly furnished. The pattern suggests that elites may have controlled or benefited from lead production while lower-status households worked more directly with ore processing and smelting. Children growing up in those households would consequently have faced greater exposure.
Isotopic analysis indicated that most of the individuals studied had grown up locally. This suggests that mining and smelting knowledge passed through generations within relatively stable communities, rather than the industry depending on large numbers of incoming workers.
Merrony said, “Our recent excavations in Castleton have provided a lot of new information about the people living in the Hope Valley during the medieval period. We now understand more about the size of the population in the valley, and we can see from the archaeological evidence that these working communities were involved in industries that required hard physical labor. However, this study has enabled us, for the first time, to see beyond this broader understanding and to look more deeply into the profound impact lead production had on individuals and the communities they lived in.”
Lead’s possible toll on young women
Lead can damage the nervous system, kidneys, and reproductive system, making the childhood exposures a concern even for people who survived for many years afterward. Three women analyzed in the study had elevated childhood lead exposure and died between approximately 17 and 25 years of age. The relationship between childhood exposure and premature death is complex, so these findings suggest a possible association with increased health risks without establishing that lead caused their deaths. Pregnancy may have been a particularly vulnerable time because lead stored in the body can be released back into the bloodstream.
Dr. Anna Bloxam, co-director of the Castleton excavations, said, “We know from modern studies that lead can have profoundly harmful effects on the health and development of children: there is no safe level of exposure. All the individuals included in our study survived into adulthood, but they were exposed to lead while they were young and growing. We can tell from their skeletons that most of the men we studied lived until middle or old age, whereas the women primarily died much earlier, in young adulthood.
“Our results indicate that in these mining communities, girls and boys alike were raised in dangerously polluted home environments. This exposure will likely have caused negative health effects in life, and perhaps contributed to higher rates of premature death among women of childbearing age.”
The findings concern medieval mining and smelting between the seventh and 15th centuries and do not describe modern environmental conditions. The legacy of historic mining in the Peak District is now well understood and carefully monitored, with land management, conservation, and environmental regulation helping to minimize risks associated with former mining activity.
The results will contribute to the developing medieval archaeological research agenda for the Peak District National Park. A temporary display in the region during fall and winter 2026–27 will present the research alongside archaeological discoveries from the Castleton excavations.
Reference: “Social dynamics of toxic metal industry in medieval Europe: Peak District lead production, AD 600–1500” by Christopher P. Loveluck, Hannah J. O’Regan, Anna Bloxam, Catrin Fear, Jane Evans, Simon Chenery, Carolyn Chenery, Colin Merrony, Fiona E. Moore and Angela Darlington, 13 October 2026,
Antiquity
DOI: 10.15184/aqy.2026.10416
The research was funded and supported by the University of Nottingham, the Peak District National Park Authority, Castleton Historical Society, the University of Sheffield, Sheffield Museums and Historic England.

title: Eating 30% Less Food Has an Unexpected Effect on DNA, Study Finds
content:
New research in mice reveals how reducing food intake can influence DNA across the genome, potentially pointing toward new ways to protect cells as they age. Credit: Shutterstock
A study reveals that calorie restriction affects genetic mutations differently across tissues and regions of DNA.
Eating fewer calories may do more than slow certain aspects of aging. Scientists have found that mice consuming 30 percent less food accumulated fewer DNA mutations across several tissues, suggesting that diet can influence how genetic damage builds up over time.
The study, published in
, examined mutations across a large portion of the genome rather than focusing on individual genes. The results showed that calorie restriction affected different organs and regions of DNA in surprisingly different ways.
How Eating Less Affects DNA Mutations
DNA mutations develop throughout life as cells experience genetic damage or make mistakes while copying and repairing their DNA. Most mutations are harmless, but some interfere with normal gene function and can contribute to cancer and other diseases. Although animal studies have established that calorie restriction can extend lifespan and slow certain effects of aging, its broader influence on mutation accumulation has remained unclear.
To investigate, researchers led by NYU Langone Health and University Hospitals Cleveland worked with scientists at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and the National Institutes of Health. Using highly accurate DNA sequencing technology, they examined genetic changes in mice fed 30 percent fewer calories than animals allowed to eat freely.
The restricted diet reduced several types of mutations, including substitutions, which occur when one DNA letter is replaced by another, and insertions and deletions, which add or remove DNA letters. However, the reductions differed across tissues, with liver cells showing a stronger response than kidney or brain cells.
“While links between diet and lifespan have been established in animals, our results show that diet and mutations across the genome are also linked,” said co-corresponding study author Gilad D. Evrony, MD, PhD, a researcher at NYU Langone Health and associate professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “Mice on a calorie-restricted diet are healthier for longer, but this diet is too challenging for humans. Nevertheless, considering the role mutations play in cancer and many other diseases, it’s exciting to have found a way to decrease mutations, which we can now work to understand.”
The Unexpected Pattern Hidden Across the Genome
The researchers also discovered that calorie restriction did not affect all regions of DNA equally. In liver and kidney cells, the greatest reductions in mutations occurred in the least active portions of the genome. These regions contain either no genes or genes that are not being used by the cells.
One possible explanation involves differences in DNA repair activity. Regions containing actively used genes already undergo frequent DNA repair, which may limit how much additional protection they receive if calorie restriction reduces DNA damage. Less active regions, where repair occurs less frequently, could experience a larger reduction in accumulated mutations. The researchers have not yet established whether this mechanism explains the pattern.
“We didn’t expect to find this asymmetry across the genome,” said co-corresponding author Jonathan Shoag, MD, an associate professor in the Department of Urology at University Hospitals Cleveland and Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine. “By profiling more dietary interventions and mutations in additional tissues and cell types, we hope to learn what drives the connection between diet and mutations.”
Could Genetic Damage Be Reduced Without Extreme Dieting?
The findings establish a connection between calorie restriction and lower mutation levels in mice, but they do not demonstrate that people would experience the same benefits. Sustained, substantial calorie restriction is also difficult to maintain and can carry health risks.
Researchers now hope to identify the biological processes responsible for the reduction in mutations. Understanding those processes could help scientists investigate approaches that protect DNA without requiring people to follow severely restricted diets.
“Understanding these mechanisms could eventually reveal new ways to reduce mutations – without the challenges and risks of an extreme diet—to counter diseases of aging,” said first study author Marta Grońska-Pęski, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow in Evrony’s laboratory.
The research relied on a specially established group of mice used to study the biological effects of calorie restriction. “We were fortunate to have collaborated with Dr. Victoria Acosta-Rodríguez, Dr. Joseph Takahashi, and Dr. Carla Green, who established this mouse caloric restriction cohort,” said Dr. Evrony.
Reference: “Caloric restriction modulates genome-wide somatic mutation in mice” by Marta Grońska-Pęski, Victoria Acosta-Rodríguez, Amoolya Srinivasa, Amanda Garrido, Shany Picciotto, Carla B. Green, Joseph S. Takahashi, Jonathan E. Shoag and Gilad D. Evrony, 9 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.013
This work was supported by National Institutes of Health grants T32AG052909, F32AG076287, and UH3NS132024, the Pew Charitable Trusts, the Jacob Goldfield Foundation, the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation, the Smythe Family Impact Fund, the Vail family, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

title: Tiny Atomic Defects Reveal a Quantum Secret Hidden Inside an Unusual Metal
content:
In a metal, electrons normally move freely through the crystal like waves rippling across the sea, but under the right quantum conditions they can be trapped in place, according to new research from Columbia University. Credit: Raquel Queiroz, Columbia University.
Atomic-scale defects in an unusual metal may offer a new way to control quantum states.
Scientists at
Columbia University
have discovered that electron waves can become trapped inside a metal, even when pathways remain available for them to escape. The finding, published in
, provides the first experimental evidence of a long-predicted quantum phenomenon in a metallic material.
The trapped waves were found near atomic defects in a metal called Pd5AlI2. Unlike electrons that move freely through conducting materials, these waves remain confined because of quantum interference.
“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2. What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal,” said Columbia theoretical physicist Raquel Queiroz.
How Quantum Interference Traps Electrons
Quantum mechanics describes electrons as waves that can travel along multiple possible paths. When these waves overlap, they can reinforce or cancel one another. Under certain conditions, destructive interference can prevent an electron wave from spreading, even when other electron states can move through the same material.
This phenomenon is called a bound state in the continuum (BIC). “Quantum mechanics predicts that an electron wave can, theoretically, remain trapped even when there are infinitely many paths for it to escape. This effect is known from light waves, but it has never been seen before for electrons,” said Queiroz.
An Unusual Metal Reveals a Quantum Effect
The discovery began in Columbia chemist Xavier Roy’s laboratory, where researchers developed Pd5AlI2, a metal that can be separated into thin, two-dimensional layers while retaining its metallic properties. Measurements showed that its electrons moved more slowly than expected.
Working with Queiroz and experimental physicists Cory Dean and Aravind Devarakonda (a former Columbia postdoc who is now an assistant professor of applied physics at Columbia), the team traced this behavior to electron hopping frustration. The metal’s atomic structure creates competing paths for electrons to move between atoms, allowing destructive interference to suppress their movement. The findings were published in
Nature Physics
Spectroscopic images of the 2D metal Pd5AlI2 revealing bound electron waves around atomic defects. These are the first observations of a bound state in the continuum (BIC) in a metal. Credit: Morgan Thinel, Pasupathy Lab/Columbia University
Researchers working with Columbia physicist Abhay Pasupathy later detected unexpected patterns while examining Pd5AlI2 using atomic-scale scanning and spectroscopy techniques. Further analysis revealed electron waves trapped near defects in the crystal lattice. Queiroz developed theoretical models explaining how quantum interference produced these localized states.
Potential Applications in Quantum Technology
Bound states in the continuum have previously been demonstrated with light, where they have helped advance lasers, optical sensing, and nonlinear optics. The Columbia findings establish that a similar effect can occur with electrons in metals.
“Trapping a wave is an idea as old as quantum mechanics itself, but it took almost a century to figure out how to do it with light. We have now realized it with electrons in a material,” said Roy. “And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it.”
Electronic bound states could eventually contribute to highly sensitive quantum sensors, quantum information processing, and quantum chemistry. However, controlling their formation remains a challenge.
In Pd5AlI2, the electron traps form around defects that arise randomly during crystal growth. Roy and Pasupathy are now investigating ways to deliberately position these defects and control the resulting interference patterns. The discovery also offers a way to identify other metals with frustrated crystal structures that could support trapped electron waves.

title: Scientists Develop a Clever New Way To Kill Cancer Cells From the Inside
content:
Chemistry
Artistic rendering of the study’s achievement: cancer-killing drug formation using excess carbon monoxide found inside cancer cells. Credit: RIKEN
Scientists have developed an experimental strategy that exploits a chemical byproduct of cancer cells to produce anticancer drugs directly inside them.
Scientists in Japan have developed an experimental method that uses a chemical produced by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer drugs directly inside them. The approach relies on carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that certain tumors produce in unusually high amounts, to activate a chemical reaction designed to destroy cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy tissue.
In a proof-of-concept study published in
Nature Communications
, researchers at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) demonstrated that their system could generate drug compounds selectively in cultured cancer cells. The findings suggest a possible alternative to conventional chemotherapy, although the technique has not yet been tested in animals or humans.
Turning a Cancer Byproduct Into a Treatment
Carbon monoxide is best known as a poisonous gas released during incomplete combustion, including in vehicle exhaust. However, the human body also produces small amounts of it naturally. Research has shown that many types of cancer cells generate elevated levels, creating a chemical difference that could potentially be exploited for targeted treatment.
A team led by Katsunori Tanaka investigated whether this excess carbon monoxide could serve as a raw material for producing anticancer compounds inside tumors. Their strategy uses palladacycles, organometallic compounds containing palladium, to convert carbon monoxide into a molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain phenanthridinone derivatives are toxic to cells and have been used in anticancer drugs.
This study’s major achievement. After sending the albumin-palladocycle complex into cancer cells, the albumin was able to protect the palladium catalyst from glutathione. This allowed the catalyst to remain viable, and excess carbon monoxide within cancer cells could then be used to produce the drug, which was then freed up to kill the cancer cells. Credit: RIKEN
Protecting a Delicate Chemical Reaction
The researchers faced a significant obstacle: palladium catalysts are rapidly deactivated by substances naturally present inside cells, including glutathione. Without protection, the catalyst would lose its ability to carry out the drug-producing reaction.
To solve this problem, the team enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, an abundant protein found in blood. Albumin acts as a protective carrier, shielding the palladium catalyst from molecules that would otherwise disable it. The resulting albumin complex can circulate through the bloodstream and remain chemically active after entering cells.
After screening several palladacycles to identify the most effective candidate, the researchers tested the protected complex against human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cell lines, along with a noncancerous cell line.
Cancer Cells Produce the Drug Compounds
Following 48 hours of incubation, the researchers detected the intended phenanthridinone product in all four cancer cell lines but not in the noncancerous cells. The results indicated that the protected catalyst remained functional and that the reaction depended on chemical conditions associated with the cancer cells.
The team then refined the system to allow the newly synthesized compound to separate from its carrier and move freely within the cell. Further modifications enabled the production of a highly toxic phenanthridinone derivative used in anticancer drugs. When tested in liver cancer cells, the modified system generated the toxic compound internally, causing harmful effects in those cells.
Another concern was whether carbon monoxide already present in blood might activate drug production before the complex reached a tumor. Blood tests showed no detectable formation of the toxic compound. The researchers suggested that carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells, was unavailable to participate in the reaction.
The Next Step Toward Targeted Cancer Therapy
Rather than administering a finished anticancer drug, Tanaka’s approach aims to deliver relatively harmless chemical components that become toxic only after encountering suitable conditions inside diseased cells.
“This work represents an important advance in therapeutic
synthetic chemistry,” says Tanaka. “In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body—including disease-associated metabolites—are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease.”
The researchers’ next step is to test the method in animal models, where they can investigate whether the catalyst reaches tumors, produces sufficient amounts of the drug, and avoids damaging healthy tissues.
Reference: “Harnessing endogenous carbon monoxide for cancer-selective drug synthesis” by Masayuki Kawai, Tsung-Che Chang, Ambara R. Pradipta and Katsunori Tanaka, 17 September 2026,
Nature Communications

title: Researchers scale flexible perovskite modules to 750 cm² with certified 20.2% efficiency
content:
Researchers scale flexible perovskite modules to 750 cm² with certified 20.2% efficiency
Researchers at Soochow University, Southeast University, Linköping University, the Institute of Chemistry of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and
SunFlex New Energy
have developed a way to make large flexible perovskite solar modules that keep most of the efficiency of small cells. The modules are built on flexible PET/ITO substrates.
Efficiency and stability have typically dropped sharply as flexible perovskite devices get larger, and the problem lies at the substrate surface. On flexible ITO, the hydroxyl groups that anchor the self-assembled monolayer (SAM) hole-transport molecule, Me-4PACz, are fewer and less uniform, and they are quickly lost in the polar precursor solution. The perovskite colloids also interact with the SAM’s phosphonic acid groups, which slows SAM anchoring until the hydroxyls are gone. The team added a “decoupling agent”, 3,5-bis(methylsulfonyl)phenylammonium iodide (BSAI), to the precursor. It binds to the lead-iodide species, weakens their interaction with the SAM so the SAM anchors quickly and uniformly, and also slows perovskite nucleation to promote oriented crystal growth.
Third-party certified efficiencies were 26.9% for small-area flexible cells (against 26.22% previously reported), 22.3% for a 14.55 cm² device, 20.6% for an 80 cm² device and 20.2% for a 750 cm² module. The certified 750 cm² device used a phenethylammonium iodide passivator. With a different passivator, 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide, a 14.55 cm² device with 22.0% efficiency lost about 8% after 1,044 hours of maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices also passed all test sequences of the IEC TS 63163:2021 standard for flexible portable modules, as certified by TÜV SÜD. The approach also works on rigid substrates and with other SAM molecules.
The team worked with SunFlex for about a year to scale production beyond laboratory prototypes. SunFlex was founded by Yongfang Li, one of the paper’s authors, and builds on perovskite research at Soochow University.

title: TNO, Perovion and Toyo Seikan sign Statement of Intent to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells
content:
TNO, Perovion and Toyo Seikan sign Statement of Intent to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells
Perovion Technologies
and Toyo Seikan Group Holdings have signed a Statement of Intent to advance their joint development of lightweight, flexible perovskite solar cells toward industrialization. The signing took place at a ceremony at the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The three organizations had already been working together on the technology and on opportunities for practical application, and have now agreed on a joint development roadmap.
Under the roadmap, they will collaborate on technology development, materials development, manufacturing processes and module technologies. Perovion contributes the flexible perovskite solar cell technology developed at TNO and its scalable roll-to-roll manufacturing approach. Toyo Seikan will bring its expertise in advanced functional materials, developed under its MiraNeo brand, as well as its know-how in manufacturing and module integration.
Perovion’s CEO Stefan van de Beek pointed in particular to Toyo Seikan’s encapsulation materials. TNO remains involved as technology and R&D partner, supporting further development and scale-up. The release does not give financial terms, a timeline or production targets.
Perovion is a TNO spin-off, launched in March 2026, that aims to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells printed on thin foils. It plans a roll-to-roll factory in the Netherlands, with construction planned for 2030, and said at launch that it was seeking investors and industrial partners. TNO also recently unveiled a

活动聚焦光伏发电工程建设、设备质量、安全运维、节能降耗、并网管理等重点标准内容，通过线下宣讲、展板宣传、发放科普资料、企业走访答疑等多种形式，面向新能源企业、在建光伏项目、产业园区及社会群众开展标准化宣传。重点解读光伏发电国家、行业及先进地方标准规范，讲解标准化在提升光伏项目安全性、经济性、稳定性中的重要作用，引导经营主体严格按照标准开展建设、运维和管理。

title: 天津：“十五五”新增用电全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决-索比光伏网
content:
10月22日上午，天津市政府新闻办举行“开局起步‘十五五’”系列主题新闻发布会，介绍“十五五”时期我市能源发展有关情况。
市发展改革委主任梁军介绍，能源保障和安全事关国计民生。“十四五”以来，天津深入践行“四个革命、一个合作”能源安全新战略，着力强基础、调结构、优布局、育动能，能源高质量发展迈出坚实步伐。“十四五”期间，能源发展成效主要体现在四个方面。一是保障能力更强，渤海油田稳居全国第一大原油生产基地，原油增量占全国总增量的约40%。电力供应水平稳步提高，电力装机较2020年增长73.7%。二是能源结构更绿，新能源超过煤电成为第一大电源，煤炭消费比重由34.6%下降至24.6%，非化石能源消费比重由7.1%提高至17%，绿电交易连续三年倍速增长。三是设施布局更优，天然气主干架构持续巩固，三座LNG接收站投产运行，接收能力领跑全国。特高压输电网络加速构建，500千伏电网建成双环网结构。四是发展动能更新，获批京津冀燃料电池汽车示范城市群，打造天津港保税区氢能示范产业园，依托荣程集团等企业加快交通领域氢能应用场景建设，燃料电池实证试验平台纳入国家首批能源领域氢能试点，“制储运加用”氢能全产业链发展格局加快形成。
“十五五”时期是我国加快构建新型能源体系、建设能源强国的重要时期。我们将认真落实党中央决策部署和国家发展改革委、国家能源局工作要求，以保安全、优结构、强产业、降成本为主线，着力打造区域能源保障枢纽和能源领域新质生产力发展引领区，到2030年，初步建成以非化石能源为增量供应主体、化石能源为兜底保障、新型电力系统为关键支撑、绿色智慧节约为用能导向的清洁低碳安全高效的新型能源体系，更好支撑经济社会高质量发展。为了实现以上目标，我们在任务安排方面突出“四个着力”。
一是着力筑牢能源安全根基，全面提升综合保障能力。加强与煤炭主产区合作，扎实做好煤炭稳供保运。大力推动渤海油田、大港油田稳产增储，打造全国油气资源保障供给中心和重要LNG接收区;建成天津LNG外输管道复线等项目，持续巩固国产气、进口气相结合，陆上气、LNG相补充的多源多向供气保障格局。健全多层次能源储备体系，强化天然气、成品油、煤炭等能源储备，扎实推进大港油田储气库群项目建设，力争储气库工作气量达到50亿立方米。增强供热、燃气综合保障能力，改造供热管网3000公里以上、燃气管网2000公里以上。
二是着力推进绿色低碳发展，强化生产消费协同转型。统筹推进风电、光伏等非化石能源开发，实施蓟州“风光火热储”多能互补一体化等试点，非化石能源发电装机超过2000万千瓦，装机比重超过50%;持续扩大省间绿电交易，谋划新增绿电入津通道，“十五五”时期新增用电需求全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决。全面落实大气污染治理攻坚行动部署，加快化石能源消费绿色转型，高水平高质量做好节能降碳，煤炭消费总量较2025年下降10%、比重降至21%左右，非化石能源消费比重增至22.2%。
三是着力构建新型电力系统，推进供给水平质效双升。发挥好传统火电兜底保障作用，进一步提高外受电规模，有序实施杨柳青电厂、大唐盘山电厂容量替代，电力装机超过4000万千瓦。抢抓“六张网”建设机遇，打造新型电网平台，建成大同—天津南特高压交流输电工程，推进黑龙江—天津特高压直流输电工程实施，构建“三交一直”特高压输电网络;建设500千伏加强型双环网，推进电网数字化智能化转型。加快蓟州龙潭沟、西大峪抽水蓄能电站开工建设，统筹布局200万千瓦新型储能电站，推进长时储能与快速响应协同联动。提升需求侧协同能力，创新发展虚拟电厂、算电协同、车网互动等新业态。
四是着力推进科技产业创新，前瞻布局发展未来能源。发展壮大新一代风电光伏，打造风电高端装备制造产业集群、全国领先的硅片—光伏组件一体化制造业集群。积极提升新型储能产业能级，前瞻布局固态电池、钠离子电池等新型储能产业。加快构建氢能全链条产业生态，抢抓京津冀城市群氢能综合应用试点机遇，加快输氢、加氢基础设施建设，有序拓展交通、石化、建筑、钢铁等领域用氢场景，高标准建设天津港保税区氢能产业园，壮大氢能装备产业集群。培育发展绿氨、绿色甲醇、可持续航空燃料产业，打造北方国际航运绿色液体燃料加注贸易物流中心。
下一步，我们将锚定发展目标，聚焦能源强国战略导向和“双碳”要求，全力加快全市新型能源体系建设，推动区域能源保障枢纽能级持续提升、能源领域新质生产力发展聚势增效，为全面建设社会主义现代化大都市、奋力谱写中国式现代化天津篇章提供坚实能源支撑，为能源强国建设贡献天津力量。

title: Submarine cable installation begins for Sicily-Calabria power connection
content:
Submarine cable installation has begun on the "Bolano-Annunziata"
power line, a project that will connect Sicily and Calabria through a 380
kV AC electricity connection.
According to Terna the link is expected to increase electricity exchange
capacity between the island and mainland Italy to 2,000 MW, supporting
greater integration of renewable energy into the grid.
The project includes the installation of three submarine cables, each measuring
7.5 km in length and laid at depths of up to 250 metres.
According to the announcement, the project marks the first time 380 kV
alternating current submarine cables with XLPE insulation have been installed
on Italy’s national transmission grid.
Two underground cable links are also being constructed to connect the submarine
cable landings with the Annunziata and Bolano substations. The onshore
routes will extend approximately 3 km in Sicily and 500 metres in Calabria.
Construction is also progressing on the new Annunziata substation and the
expansion of the Bolano substation.
The project represents a key milestone in strengthening electricity transmission
infrastructure between Sicily and mainland Italy while enabling the continued
expansion of renewable energy capacity.

title: Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval
content:
Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval
Denmark’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities has approved a project
that will allow Bornholm’s electricity grid to be connected to the planned
Bornholm Energy Island. The decision follows a political agreement reached
in February 2026.
“Our analyses show that the solution is both technically feasible and
can contribute to a robust electricity supply," says Klaus Winther,
Vice President of System Operations at Energinet.
Energinet and TREFOR Elnet Øst are now progressing preparations for the
connection. The project aims to strengthen Bornholm’s long-term electricity
supply as demand is expected to rise through electrification, the green
transition and new business opportunities.
Bornholm is currently supplied mainly through an electricity cable to Sweden,
which is expected to remain in service until 2035. The island’s peak electricity
demand is around 50 MW, while upgrades to the Swedish connection are expected
to increase available capacity to 57 MW.
According to the announcement the project includes three new transformers
and associated facilities as part of the energy island’s electricity infrastructure.
Construction is currently expected to begin in 2027.

title: Welsh businesses invited to support Erebus floating wind project
content:
Blue Gem Wind’s Erebus
has invited Welsh businesses to play a role in the floating offshore wind
industry following the launch of its procurement strategy.
The milestone marks a significant step for the project, strengthening their
presence in Wales while supporting the development of the local offshore
wind supply chain.
According to the announcement, the procurement strategy will support the
delivery of the consented 100 MW Erebus test and demonstration project,
located off the Pembrokeshire coast.
Cabinet Minister for Economy, Connectivity and Energy Adam Price said:
“Offshore wind can bring real economic benefits to Wales, driving innovation,
creating new opportunities for businesses, and regenerating our coastal
communities.”
Construction of the project is expected to generate 700 direct jobs and
800 indirect jobs across a range of roles, including manufacturing, fabrication,
port operations, vessel services, engineering, electrical infrastructure,
and operations and maintenance.
Opportunities are available to businesses already established in the offshore
energy sector, as well as those with transferable skills in engineering,
construction, manufacturing, technology and logistics.

title: The Argument in Favor of Tranched Rounds
content: Before we get to today’s column, the big day is here: Anthropic dropped its long-awaited public S-1 filing Monday morning . Tune in today for stories from my colleagues and me that will be breaking down the most important takeaways from the filing, such as improvements in the company’s compute efficiency, details on its spending and cash burn, and interesting new disclosures that could point to an eventual end to its unusual Long-Term Benefit Trust, a group of non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues and can appoint a majority of its board. Onto today’s column... It seems like every AI startup financing these days has multiple tranches in which different investors get in at different valuations. At first, it was unusual to see just two tranches. Now we see extra-hot funding rounds with three tranches or more . It’s no secret that investors aren’t thrilled about these multi-tranche rounds (specifically, the investors that can’t get in at the lower valuation). Some of them argue that the practice allows bigger venture capital firms to flex their power and force smaller VC firms into the second, more expensive tranche. They also say it allows the startup to claim a bigger valuation, even though some or most of the new capital came in at a lower price. But founders and many investors tell me that the unique capital needs of AI companies, which are eternally starved of enough servers, is driving these unusual structures. A young startup that wants to rent around 2,500 Nvidia chips to develop new models might need to raise anywhere between $150 million to $200 million in capital just to rent those graphics processing units from a cloud provider for two years, according to an investor who has backed multiple such companies. The startup then faces two unattractive options: raise capital at a lower valuation to attract institutional investors and heavily dilute existing shareholders, or raise at a $1 billion-plus valuation to minimize dilution but turn off investors that presumably want a bigger return on their investment. Tranched rounds give founders the best of both worlds, as large corporate investors like Nvidia tend to pile into the higher-valued tranche, the investor said. In many cases, Nvidia will provide a significant chunk of capital in the higher-valued tranche, often more than 25% of the total tranche, they said. Then the question becomes how the company can get an institutional investor to lead the higher-priced, less attractive round, as Nvidia doesn’t historically lead rounds itself. (That’s for several reasons, including that Nvidia often invests in competitors, doesn’t want to be seen as setting the price for the round and likely doesn’t want to invite regulatory scrutiny for investing in its customers.) In the hottest rounds, some VCs might not have a choice than to invest in or lead the more expensive round. In other cases, more unusual things might happen. One investor told me their firm will sometimes put the vast majority of their investment into the lower-priced tranche, but then will invest a few million into the higher-priced tranche and “lead” it in name only. That way, it gives corporate investors the cover to pour millions of dollars into the more expensive tranche without having to take on the responsibility of “leading” it and facing scrutiny if the startup goes south, the investor said. title: Stripe’s AI Shopping Lead Puts Card Giants on Edge
content: As AI assistants like Instinct and Meta Platforms’ Muse start to gain traction in shopping, Stripe has taken a leading position in how the agents pay. That’s putting the credit card giants on edge. The reason for their apprehension: Stripe in many cases is enabling AI agent purchases through virtual cards for one-time use, which can leave card networks with less control over the shopping and payment process, people who work closely with the card firms say. Mastercard and Visa have developed their own payment technology for agent shopping that would use customers’ existing cards, giving the card companies more visibility into who’s making what purchases. That method is still at an early stage, though. When people shop online themselves, they typically enter their card details or choose a saved payment method at checkout. But when an agent makes a purchase, it needs a way to handle shoppers’ payment information securely and use it across different retailers. Agents also need guardrails to ensure they don’t make accidental splurges. Meta and Instinct both have found a solution to those needs in Stripe’s Link digital wallet, which securely stores the users’ own card or bank account details. To enable the agent making a payment, Stripe issues a single-use virtual card that has a spending limit tied to a purchase the user has approved. The agent never sees the users’ actual card number, and the card’s limit keeps the agent from overspending. The merchant accepts the virtual card as it would any other card payment, while Stripe separately charges the user’s credit card to cover the cost of the purchase. That process creates two card transactions for a given purchase and can make it harder to connect the user with the actual purchase the agent makes. One person familiar with Mastercard’s thinking said agents’ use of virtual cards has created concerns in part because it can make it harder for card networks, banks and merchants to track transactions from start to finish and resolve disputed charges. Card networks and banks rely on users’ transaction histories to spot risky or fraudulent transactions. The use of virtual cards also puts Stripe in an advantageous position in AI shopping. It could gain more insight into people’s agentic shopping habits than the card networks currently can, since Stripe can see what people are buying through the AI agents it supports. And its early foothold could give it more sway than the card networks over how the technology evolves. “For Visa and Mastercard, the biggest risk to their business is Stripe infrastructure becoming the default solution,” said Rene Reinsberg, CEO and co-founder of Self, a startup that builds identity and payments tools for AI agents. “I think that’s even more pronounced with agentic commerce than the traditional commerce checkout flows.” Shopping with agents is still in its infancy, but it has begun to take off with early AI adopters. Last week, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, for instance, told investors that more than a quarter of the 10 million users of Muse are shopping with the app, making commerce its most popular use. The average size of Muse transactions is over $200, he said. The demand for shopping with the app has so exceeded Meta’s expectations that it had to work with Stripe in the week after Muse launched to raise credit limits due to high shopping volumes, Zuckerberg said. In another wrinkle, Stripe could switch an agent’s card to a different card network from the shopper’s original card—for instance, the agent might pay with a Visa virtual card that’s funded by the user’s Mastercard card. That could divert transactions and fees away from the card network for the shopper’s original card. Stripe works with both Visa and Mastercard in its broader card issuing business, though it isn’t clear how transaction volume is divided between the card giants for virtual card agentic payments. Visa and Mastercard, for their part, are promoting their own alternative to virtual cards by creating digital tokens tied to shoppers’ existing cards that authorized agents can use to make purchases. The tokens identify the end user without the agent handling sensitive card information directly. Both card giants are courting AI companies and merchants to use their respective payment systems, Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay. Visa, for example, launched a pilot with Bill and Billtrust, companies that help businesses manage or collect payments, that allows authorized agents to pay invoices approved by buyers. Visa and Mastercard also partnered with Anthropic to help merchants build their own AI shopping assistants using Claude technology. While the technology is already in use in some transactions and pilot launches—and Stripe has added support for Visa and Mastercard tokens—adoption remains limited overall. But the card networks may have an edge in winning over card-issuing banks to the token system. The banks are another crucial part of card payments and would be key allies because they control the approval that determines whether card transactions happen at all. Last month, Bank of America and five other banks published proposed industry guidelines that appeared to favor the card networks’ preferred approach over Stripe’s use of virtual cards. The banks called for “auditable methods to enter payment credentials.” The banks didn’t call out virtual cards specifically as a risk, but they did warn about agentic payment methods that make it harder to connect a purchase to an actual shopper or merchant. Stripe, for its part, says it has worked closely with its card network partners on its current technology. “Stripe built this [virtual card] capability in consultation with our network partners and will continue to work closely with them as standards for agentic commerce evolve,” a Stripe spokesperson said. A Mastercard spokesperson said different payment methods could “coexist” as agentic commerce matures, but Mastercard believes over the long term that “the model will increasingly be tokenized transactions routed directly with the merchant.” That approach “preserves the right information flow between the consumer, merchant and issuer, supports clearer dispute resolution, and allows the merchant of record to manage the relationship with the cardholder,” the Mastercard spokesperson said. Visa didn’t have a comment.
