title: Anthropic’s Big Reveal
content: The tech industry equivalent of the Super Bowl may finally be upon us. Anthropic could make public the paperwork for its initial public offering as early as Monday. Details about Anthropic’s finances from either drafts of the IPO filing or recent investor meetings have been dribbling out for weeks. As a result, some of the S-1’s revelations will not be, well, all that revelatory. But there are still many, many mysteries about Anthropic the filing could clear up, or at least make a little less fuzzy. I asked my colleagues Jason Dean and Laura Mandaro for their shortlist of items they hope the S-1 will illuminate: • More financial details. More clarity on Anthropic’s trajectory toward profitability, along with cash flow numbers and other operational financial metrics that haven’t yet leaked out. • Ownership, investment and revenue details from big partners. Hopefully, the filing will confirm just how much money Anthropic is paying Google and Amazon to run its AI on their servers, along with details about how much those companies invested in Anthropic and how much those stakes have appreciated. • Who pays Anthropic’s bills. Anthropic has said around a fifth of its revenue this quarter of its revenue in the first half of this year came from just two customers, compared to a quarter for all of 2025, according to published reports. Investors will look for more recent concentration data and additional details on the sources of its revenue. Historically, most of its revenue has come from sales of its AI via an application programming interface, but these can rise and fall depending on what model is hot among developers. We’re looking for details on revenue from its Claude subscriptions as well as through other companies like Amazon that resell Anthropic AI in exchange for a cut of those sales . • More on governance. Many idiosyncrasies of Anthropic’s mission-minded corporate structure are public. For instance, a group of non-shareholders called the Long-Term Benefit Trust appoints the majority of its board. As we’ve reported , in the run-up to the IPO, Anthropic developed a plan to grant its seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, a combined 50.1% of voting power even if they reduce some of their stakes. What we don’t know is whether Amodei has any particular power over the six other founders and how exactly Anthropic will resolve conflicts between the trust and board members appointed by the founders. (Anthropic has planned to give employees a special class of stock for tiebreaker votes—complicated!) • Lockups and secondary sales. We’ve written that Anthropic has mulled extending the lockups —the period when most shareholders are barred from selling their stock—beyond the typical 180-day period. But the company has considered making an exception for some shareholders at the time of the IPO, allowing what’s known as a secondary sale at the listing. Such sales would contrast with other tech IPOs this year that didn’t allow secondary sales during their listings, such as SpaceX and Cerebras. We’re looking for how long most investors have to sit on their shares and which groups of investors—or employees—can bail more quickly. More Ahead The Anthropic filing fireworks aren’t the only big events in tech we’ll be watching next week. There’s also: • Earnings reports from the three major hyperscalers. Google and Microsoft are scheduled to report on Wednesday, while Amazon will report on Thursday. Any changes the companies announce to their data center spending plans or forecasts about AI demand are likely to move the already jittery markets. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy isn’t waiting until earnings to strike a bullish note on the performance of AWS, his cloud unit. In an Andreessen Horowitz podcast published Friday, Jassy said AWS is “largely sold out” of computing capacity through the end of next year. He also said the company’s decade-old acquisition of Annapurna Labs, a semiconductor startup behind AWS’ custom AI chip and other processors, may end up being Amazon’s best deal ever. • Instacart’s next move. On Friday, we broke the news that Instacart is exploring a possible sale of the company and has held preliminary conversations with DoorDash and Uber. Our story said that talks with Uber appear to have fizzled. But it will be interesting to see if a deal with someone else comes together. Instacart and DoorDash are due to report earnings on Nov. 5 and 4, respectively. Expect analysts to grill the companies about the prospects for a deal, if one isn’t announced by then. • New Apple devices. Apple is having an event on Wednesday where it’s expected to announce its first touchscreen MacBook, as we mentioned earlier in the week . Get ready for some greasy MacBook screens. title: Exclusive: Inside Unusual Machines' $52 Million Drone Battery Acquisition
content: In 2020, Matt Barnard built a drone by hand at his home in Missouri and thought he had the perfect buyers for it: cattle ranchers in neighboring Oklahoma, who he knew had a heck of a time keeping track of their grazing herds. Using drones equipped with cameras, ranchers could follow their cattle on their laptops. But then the ranchers came up with a competing way to locate the cattle—GPS devices clipped to the animals’ ears—and lost any interest in Barnard’s drones. If he couldn’t sell drones, Barnard thought he might be able to produce and sell the primary component that makes them go—batteries. He launched a startup designing battery packs specifically for drones. The bet paid off last week, when Barnard closed the sale of that startup, Upgrade Energy, to Florida drone component supplier Unusual Machines for $52 million in cash and stock. It was a coup for Barnard, who told me he had entirely bootstrapped the business and raised no venture capital or debt. The deal was also a big get for Unusual Machines, which added to its muscle as the leading supplier of U.S.-made drone components to companies competing in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program for $1.1 billion in contracts. Chinese manufacturers such as DJI make most of the world’s drones, along with the components that go into them. But the Pentagon, seeking to build up a U.S. drone industry and wean the country off Chinese suppliers, has sharply restricted the use of Chinese-made components by Drone Dominance participants. In the latest stage of the Drone Dominance competition last month, Unusual Machines supplied components to four of the nine companies that placed, including top winners Perennial Autonomy, founded by former Google Chair Eric Schmidt, and Neros Technologies. The acquisition of Upgrade Energy, which is also a supplier to Perennial and Neros, bulks up Unusual Machines’ manufacturing capacity with the most expensive single component in a drone—the battery. Unusual Machines’ shares are up 21% since it announced the deal in May, and they’ve risen 32% over the last year. “We exist because we took this gamble and people invested in this gamble,” Allan Evans, CEO of Unusual Machines, told me. “We’re a little past it being a gamble—it’s worked out and now we’re scaling.” I visited Upward’s factory in Torrance, Calif., earlier this month. It’s a large, white-painted space in an industrial park where after work a group of young men sitting on a couch huddled together over a videogame and otherwise hung out. The factory itself was through a door in the back. There, in rows of desks packed with electronics, some 50 workers package next-generation cylindrical cells from Taiwan’s Molicel, Calif.–based Amprius Technologies and others in black, rectangular packs small enough to hold in one hand. They then box them up and move them on pallets to a loading dock. Barnard said they are pumping out 400 packs a day. Next-generation battery startups began to pop up in the late 2000s and the early 2010s, triggered by improvements in lithium-ion batteries and especially the rise of Tesla. In 2020 and 2021, a slew of them went public on the general expectation of an electric vehicle boom. But EV sales beyond Tesla remained sluggish. The industry is only now coming out of that malaise. The drone boom, along with the mania over AI data centers, have been the main life preservers for these startups, as we have reported . But Barnard has been in the business longer than most, pumping out drone packs. His big insight was to avoid the risks most of the other battery startups took in attempting to invent and scale up a new battery chemistry or component. He decided to take some of the best of what was already out there—like the batteries made by Molicel and Amprius, with their next-generation silicon anodes—and figure out how to package them optimally for drones. He then got those packs in front of drone makers. In 2023, Barnard said, he got a deal to power drones that delivered food in Georgia for Papa Johns Pizza. The same year, he landed his first significant deal—a contract to supply Neros, at the time a small drone maker based in El Segundo, Calif. Based on that contract, Barnard decided to move Upgrade from Missouri to Southern California. He and his father packed up his things, stuffed them into a big truck, and drove to the state. With three employees, they moved into a space in Compton, Calif. Upgrade got some press when it powered a solar aircraft making a round-the-world flight. Last year, orders for batteries to power combat drones started rolling in. Barnard continued to get business from Neros, which had become one of the country’s main drone manufacturers, and now also had business with Anduril and AeroVironment, he said. Near the end of last year, Evans came around. Barnard recalls Evans saying that Unusual Machines wanted to begin building batteries. “I said, ‘OK, cool. What do you want to do?’ And they’re like, ‘Acquire you.’” “‘Ah, OK, great,’” Barnard recalls responding. Evans said he had to take Barnard out for meals before he could close the deal. “Initially he was like, ‘Nah.’ And so we had dinner a couple of nights,” he said. Evans stressed that he could promise Barnard a ton of business and expansion. “We have the buying volume to be an anchor customer for somebody to move cell production to the U.S.,” he recalled telling Barnard. “We have the ability to automate and scale. We have the ability to put batteries into thousands of drones.” That turned Barnard around. “Now I’m not competing against some other company that just raised $10 million, $20 million, when I did not have $10 million or $20 million sitting around,” Barnard said. “I recognized that to stay competitive, I needed to attach myself to some of that funding. I’m glad I did.” ----- Noteworthy General Motors led a $108 million Series B round in sodium-ion battery systems provider Peak Energy. GM and Peak are developing sodium-ion batteries for deployment on the grid. In total, Peak has raised $173 million in equity funding. High-nickel battery maker Forge Nano went public in a merger with a special purpose acquisition corporation, highlighting the revival of new stock listings in the battery industry after a four-year downturn. The company is building a plant in Morrisville, N.C., to manufacture high-nickel batteries with either silicon or graphite anodes, and it plans to begin production in 2028. China tightened its export ban on components for large drones. The new restrictions, affecting drones and components that can be used in combat, take effect Nov. 18. ---- Recommended Newsletter Start your day with Applied AI, the newsletter that uncovers how leading businesses are leveraging AI to automate tasks. title: The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
content:
The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
Plus: Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivity.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab
We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.
A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.
As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.
Here’s why AI safety needs to go further.
Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships
Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.
A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.
The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off?
Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality.
—Robin George Andrews
This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivity

3 A personalised skin cancer vaccine is set to be approved next year
The mRNA vaccine showed great promise in trials. (New Scientist $)
+ Companies are playing word games with vaccines. (MIT Technology Review)
4 OpenAI is now training frontier models without internet access
It paused training after models breached external systems. (Bloomberg $)
+ Training will now take place offline to reduce security risks. (TechCrunch)
+ Its agents can still communicate without a network connection. (Verge)
5 US lawmakers are preparing for possible AI-driven mass layoffs
A new bill would extend jobless aid and retraining support. (NYT $)
+ But what do the numbers actually say about AI’s impact on jobs? (MIT Technology Review)
6 The first foldable iPhone is drawing buyers…and criticism
Reviewers praised its inner screen but criticised its outer one. (WSJ $)
+ Peter Thiel says Apple has done 'nothing new' after Steve Jobs. (BI)
7 Iran has threatened to target Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
Officials said Tehran would disrupt internet connections. (Reuters $)
8 New UFO files detail a strange, flying "black triangle”
FBI documents describe a 15-foot object moving at fighter-jet speed. (Axios)
+ It’s never been easier to be a conspiracy theorist. (MIT Technology Review)
9 The BBC’s Blue Planet III left flaws in its footage to prove it’s not AI
Producers used murkier shots to reinforce the series’ authenticity. (Guardian)
10 Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey has arrived—to scorn and ridicule
Viewers derided Grok’s first AI-generated episode. (TechCrunch)
Quote of the day
“It's very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry.”
—Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) tells Axios that bombastic claims from AI leaders are failing to win over the public.
One more thing
A woman’s uterus has been kept alive outside the body for the first time
Ten months ago, reproductive health researchers placed a freshly donated human uterus inside a new device they call “Mother.” They connected the organ to the machine’s plastic veins and arteries and pumped in modified human blood.
The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story.
—Jessica Hamzelou
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
content:
The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
Lawmakers are passing industry-backed bills to guard against the worst outcomes, rather than addressing more common problems.
Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.
We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.
A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.
A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.
Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.
We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.
AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.
Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.
We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.
Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.
Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

content:
Rennen mit der Roten Königin: Mit Spieltheorie zu mehr Softwaresicherheit im KI-Zeitalter

Rennen mit der Roten Königin: Mit Spieltheorie zu mehr Softwaresicherheit im KI-Zeitalter
| Copyright:
CISPA/Chiara Schwarz
Download
In Lewis Carrolls Alice hinter den Spiegeln (1871), trifft Alice auf die Rote Königin und wird von ihr in ein hastiges Rennen verwickelt. In diesem wundersamen Land, erfährt Alice, muss man so schnell wie möglich laufen, nur, um auf der Stelle zu bleiben. Mit diesem „Red Queens Race“ vergleicht Christoph Landolt die Situation von Software-Herstellern im KI-Zeitalter. Denn mit den sprunghaft wachsenden Cyber-Fähigkeiten der Frontier-Modelle multiplizieren sich auch die Angriffsmöglichkeiten. Mit einem Ansatz aus der Spieltheorie hat Landolt berechnet, wie die Veröffentlichung neuer KI-Modelle sequenziert werden kann, um Software-Herstellern einen Vorsprung vor Cyberkriminellen einzuräumen.
Dass sich mit jedem neuen Release die Fähigkeiten der KI-Modelle multiplizieren, ist ein Phänomen, das Christoph Landolt beschäftigt. Er ist Doktorand in der Forschungsgruppe von CISPA-Faculty Prof. Dr. Mario Fritz und beobachtet die Veröffentlichung sogenannter Frontier-Modelle vor allem in Hinblick auf ihre Schadenspotenziale für die Cybersicherheit. „Als Claude Opus 4.6 im Februar 2026 veröffentlicht wurde, hat das Modell allein in den ersten beiden Tagen über 500 schwerwiegende Schwachstellen in Open-Source-Software gefunden. Das zeigt, wie das ganze Feld plötzlich geflutet wird mit neuen Schwachstellen“, sagt er. Kurz darauf, im April 2026, entschied sich Anthropic gegen eine allgemeine Veröffentlichung von Claude Mythos Preview, weil das Modell sich gefährlich effizient darin erwies, bislang unbekannte Sicherheitslücken zu entdecken. „Die Frage, die wir uns in unserer Forschung stellen“, sagt Landolt, „ist, wie verändert diese Dynamik die Art und Weise auf die wir Cybersicherheit im KI-Zeitalter denken müssen?“
Wie gelingt verantwortungsvolle Offenlegung im KI-Zeitalter?
Üblicherweise sorgt die sogenannte verantwortungsvolle Offenlegung für einen Vorsprung der Cybersicherheit gegenüber den Cyberkriminellen. Wenn etwa Forschende eine Schwachstelle entdecken, melden sie diese dem Software-Hersteller, der einen Patch entwickelt und veröffentlicht. Das Wissen über die Schwachstelle dringt also erst zusammen mit dem Update nach außen und die User:innen haben eine faire Chance, sich rechtzeitig zu schützen. Öffentlich verfügbare Frontier-Modelle stellen ihre offensiven und defensiven Fähigkeiten jedoch beiden Seiten gleichzeitig zur Verfügung. „Es ist schwierig zu sagen, ob die klassische Responsible Disclosure im AI-Zeitalter obsolet geworden ist“, sagt Landolt. „Aber wir wissen, dass sich die Zeit, die es braucht, um von einer offengelegten Schwachstelle zu einem Angriff zu kommen, stark reduziert hat. Die Webseite zerodayclock.com zeigte zeitweise, dass es 2018 noch rund 2,3 Jahre waren, 2026 dagegen nur noch rund 10 Stunden.“
Mit der Sequenzierung von KI-Modellen zu mehr Cybersicherheit
Diese Dynamik wirkt sich darauf aus, ob Hersteller das Schließen von Sicherheitslücken – und User:innen das Installieren von Patches – überhaupt noch als sinnhaft erachten. „Wenn die Angreifer schneller neue Schwachstellen entdecken, als die User ihre Software updaten können, beginnt das System zu oszillieren“, erklärt Landolt. Im sprichwörtlichen Red Queen’s Race fallen Software-Hersteller und -User:innen dann zurück, ganz egal, wie schnell sie laufen: „Der Nutzen, einen Patch online zu stellen wird negativ, und der Nutzen, einen Patch nicht online zu stellen, wird ebenfalls negativ. Wenn wir in diesem Bereich operieren, ist es schlecht, egal was wir tun.“ Vor diesem Hintergrund plädiert Landolt dafür, neue Frontier-Modelle schrittweise zu veröffentlichen und Software-Herstellern als Erstes Zugang zu ihnen zu gewähren: „Durch diesen Vorsprung können wir ein Incentive dafür setzen, dass alle Patches schon bereitstehen, wenn ein neues KI-Modell öffentlich zugänglich wird. So könnte ich meine Software wieder sinnvoll schützen.“
Im oben genannten Fall von Claude Mythos Preview entschied sich Anthropic zu einem ähnlichen Vorgehen: Im Rahmen von „Project Glasswing“ wurde das Modell nur ausgewählten US-Techkonzernen zugänglich gemacht. Was Landolt und seine Co-Autor:innen Tobias Lorenz, Marta Kwiatkowska und Mario Fritz in „The Oracle’s Gambit“ vorschlagen, betrifft potenziell die gesamte KI-Industrie: Mit einem Ansatz aus der Spieltheorie, dem Stackelberg-Modell, haben sie berechnet, wie man den Zugang zu neuen Frontier-Modellen optimal im Sinne der Cybersicherheit sequenzieren könnte. „Wir haben keine wissenschaftliche Literatur gefunden, die den Einfluss von neuveröffentlichten KI-Modellen auf die Cybersicherheit analysiert“, erläutert Landolt. „Deswegen haben wir ein Modell aufgestellt, das wir mit einem exakten Wert lösen können, damit wir die Validierung der Community bekommen und Rückmeldung erhalten können, ob es Dynamiken in der Praxis gibt, die wir nicht berücksichtigt haben.“
„The Oracle’s Gambit“: Ein Stackelberg-Spiel auf zwei Ebenen
Mit ihrer Umsetzung des Stackelberg-Modells präsentieren die Forschenden ein strategisches Spiel auf zwei Ebenen. Auf der ersten Ebene tritt das Frontier Lab selbst als Spieler auf. Es schlägt eine Release Policy für ein neues Frontier-Modell vor und bestimmt damit, auf welche Art und Weise die KI veröffentlicht wird. Damit legt es zugleich die Spielregeln fest, nach denen Cyberkriminelle und Software-Hersteller auf der zweiten Ebene gegeneinander antreten. In diesem zweiten Spiel entwickeln die Hersteller mithilfe der KI Patches für eine bestimmte Anzahl von Schwachstellen, während die Cyberkriminellen das Modell dazu verwenden, diese Schwachstellen auszubeuten. Dabei befinden sich die Hersteller in einem strukturellen Nachteil. „Der Verteidiger muss nicht nur Sicherheit gewährleisten, sondern auch Verfügbarkeit: Eine Schwachstelle muss erkannt, ein Patch gebaut und getestet und veröffentlicht werden“, erklärt Landolt. „Der Angreifer hat es leichter, denn ihm ist es egal, ob er einen Absturz herbeiführt.“ Zudem müssen die Hersteller entscheiden, ob sie den Patch veröffentlichen oder zurückhalten. Dies ist eine strategische Abwägung, denn ist der Patch erst einmal bekannt, kann er von der gegnerischen Seite rückentwickelt und für Exploits genutzt werden.
Sobald dieses Spiel zu einem abschließenden Wert kommt, fällt der nächste Spielzug zurück an das Frontier Lab. Es muss nun eine Veröffentlichungsstrategie finden, die das größtmögliche gesellschaftliche Wohlergehen verspricht. Im Modell von Landolt und seinen Kolleg:innen ist das Frontier Lab dabei nicht allein von Altruismus, sondern auch von wirtschaftlichen Anreizen motiviert. „Disclosure Policies bei Software-Herstellern gehen in der Regel davon aus, dass die Entwickler selbst ein maximales Interesse daran haben, ihre User zu schützen. Bei einem Frontier Lab ist die Kundenbindung aber eine andere, denn die User einer Software sind ja nicht unbedingt Kunden des Frontier Labs“, erläutert Landolt. „Unser Spiel sieht vor, dass das Frontier Lab die Opportunity Costs seines verpassten Marktanteils balanciert mit dem Welfare des ganzen Systems. Die Idee dahinter ist, dass der Reputationsverlust des Frontier Labs sehr hoch sein könnte, wenn seine Modelle für bösartige Zwecke verwendet würden.“ In „The Oracle’s Gambit“ wirken am Gemeinwohl orientierte Veröffentlichungsstrategien also zugleich wirtschaftlichen Einbußen entgegen.
Spieltheorie und Cybersicherheit: Einbezug des Gegenübers
Es ist kein Zufall, dass die Forschenden einen spieltheoretischen Ansatz gewählt haben, um eine sinnvoll sequenzierte Veröffentlichung von Frontier-Modellen zu berechnen. „Cybersecurity und Spieltheorie ist eine gängige Kombination, aus theoretischen Überlegungen heraus. Viele Optimierungsprobleme in der Mathematik gehen von einer starren Umgebung aus. Aber in der Spieltheorie versuchen wir, optimale Lösungen zu finden unter Einbezug des Gegenübers“, sagt Landolt. Dieser Einbezug eines Dritten und der Dynamik, die er in die Interaktion einbringt, hat die Forschenden bei der Modellierung des Spielablaufs jedoch vor logistische Herausforderungen gestellt. „Wenn wir alle möglichen Interaktionen zwischen Angreifer und Verteidiger berücksichtigen, wird unser Spiel zu komplex. Wir mussten also auf vereinfachte Lösungsalgorithmen oder Annahmen zurückgreifen. Und selbst für das vereinfachte Modell haben wir zwei Terrabyte Arbeitsspeicher benötigt, nur um das Spiel einmal lösen zu können.“ Das Ergebnis ihrer Berchnungen präsentieren die Forschenden heute auf der GameSec in Michigan, der weltweit einzigen Konferenz, die Themen und Expert:innen aus Spieltheorie und KI für Sicherheit vereint.

title: Sicherheits-Check: Forschungsteam untersucht kommunale E-Mail-Server im DACH-Raum
content:
Sicherheits-Check: Forschungsteam untersucht kommunale E-Mail-Server im DACH-Raum

Prof. Dr. Ronald Petrlic bei einem Vortrag auf dem IEEE Symposium on Privacy Expectations in New York Anfang Oktober 2026.
| Quelle:
Lydia Lee
Download
Nutzen Kommunen europäische E-Mail-Provider? Und wie schützen sie sich vor Angreifern im Netz? Um das herauszufinden, analysierte die Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm (Ohm) gemeinsam mit Forschenden der Universität Fribourg und der Hochschule Luzern aus der Schweiz sowie der Technischen Hochschule Ingolstadt über 15.000 E-Mail-Server von Kommunen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz.
Für ihre Analyse verwendeten die Forschenden ausschließlich öffentlich zugängliche Daten aus dem Domain Name System (DNS). Dadurch konnten sie die Tests durchführen, ohne in die untersuchten Systeme einzugreifen.
Ihrer Studie zufolge nutzen lediglich 7,2 Prozent der Kommunen in Deutschland für ihre E-Mail-Kommunikation US-Provider. Damit sind deutsche Kommunen beim Thema digitale Souveränität bereits gut aufgestellt. Auch die Stadt Nürnberg setzt auf einen europäischen E-Mail-Dienst. Anders sieht es in Österreich und der Schweiz aus. Hier liegt der Anteil bei 67 Prozent und 53,3 Prozent.
Die Wahl des Anbieters spiele vor allem mit Blick auf den Schutz sensibler Daten eine wichtige Rolle, erklärt Prof. Dr. Ronald Petrlic von der Fakultät Informatik der Ohm. Kommunale E-Mails enthalten häufig personenbezogene Informationen und weitere schützenswerte Inhalte. Werden diese über US-Anbieter verarbeitet, können sie unter bestimmten rechtlichen Voraussetzungen in den Zugriffsbereich US-amerikanischer Behörden fallen. Der CLOUD Act ermögliche es US-Strafverfolgungsbehörden, elektronische Daten von US-Unternehmen anzufordern – auch wenn diese auf Servern außerhalb der USA gespeichert sind. „Digitale Souveränität bedeutet deshalb, sich damit auseinanderzusetzen, bei welchen Anbietern kommunale Daten verarbeitet werden“, betont Petrlic.
Auch innerhalb Deutschlands gibt es hinsichtlich der digitalen Souveränität regionale Unterschiede. In Bayern liegt der Anteil an Kommunen, die ihre E-Mails über US-Provider versenden, mit 18,7 Prozent über dem bundesweiten Durchschnitt. Petrlic führt das vor allem auf die Nähe zum Microsoft-Sitz in München zurück. Das habe auch Vorteile: „In der Studie haben wir herausgefunden, dass die Kommunen, die Microsoft nutzen, eher etablierte Sicherheitslösungen, beispielsweise gegen ‚Spoofing‘, umgesetzt haben.“ Spoofing bezeichnet eine Betrugsmasche, bei der Angreifer E-Mails versenden, die scheinbar von einer offiziellen kommunalen E-Mail-Adresse stammen.
Denn neben der digitalen Souveränität legte das Forschungsteam sein Augenmerk bei der Studie auf einen weiteren Aspekt: die Cybersicherheit in Kommunen. Sie versuchten herauszufinden, wie einfach es ist, E-Mails zu verfälschen und im Namen der Kommunen zu versenden. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass dies bei vielen Verwaltungen möglich ist. Eine wesentliche Ursache hierfür ist, dass etablierte Sicherheitsstandards wie SPF, DKIM und DMARC nicht oder nicht korrekt eingesetzt werden.
„Für Kommunen ist es wichtig, sich einen Überblick zu verschaffen, welche Dienste E-Mails im Namen der Kommunen versenden“, rät Petrlic. Dafür gäbe es Monitoring-Tools, die regelmäßig über die jeweiligen Dienste und IP-Adressen informieren. So lassen sich Angreifer und Missbrauchsquellen frühzeitig erkennen. Unterstützung erhalten die Kommunen auch beim Landesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (LSI) Bayern, das bayerische Kommunen zum Thema Cybersicherheit berät. Auch das Forschungsteam der Ohm steht in regelmäßigem Austausch mit dem LSI Bayern und dem Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI).
Als Ergebnis der Studie sind zwei interaktive Karten entstanden. Interessierte können darauf einsehen, wie die einzelnen Kommunen im DACH-Raum zum Thema Digitale Souveränität und Cybersicherheit aufgestellt sind:

content:
Neues HPC-System für Klimaforschung am DKRZ wird von BULL geliefert

Das Deutsche Klimarechenzentrum (DKRZ) hat Bull, einem führenden Anbieter für Advanced Computing und KI, einen Auftrag im Wert von 40 Millionen Euro für seinen nächsten Supercomputer erteilt. Der Auftrag umfasst neben dem HPC- und Speichersystem auch Supportleistungen über fünf Jahre. Das auf der BullSequana XH3500-Plattform basierende System ist darauf ausgelegt, sowohl physikalische Simulationen als auch KI-gestützte Klimaforschung zu ermöglichen und dabei die Energieeffizienz gegenüber dem Vorgängersystem deutlich zu verbessern.
Das Hochleistungsrechnersystem für Erdsystemforschung (HLRE-5) soll voraussichtlich Anfang 2028 für die Nutzerinnen und Nutzer zur Verfügung stehen und wird in der Lage sein, zwei globale Klimasimulationen mit einer Auflösung von 5 km gleichzeitig auszuführen. Dabei soll der Energiebedarf pro simuliertem Jahr gegenüber dem derzeitigen System Levante um rund 75 Prozent sinken.
Dieses Engagement für Energieeffizienz ist nicht neu, sondern baut auf jahrelangen kontinuierlichen gemeinsamen Anstrengungen von DKRZ und Bull auf. Die aktuelle GPU-Erweiterung des Levante-Systems erreichte in den Ausgaben der Green500-Liste vom November 2025 und Juni 2026 den dritten Platz unter den energieeffizientesten Supercomputern der Welt. Die ersten beiden Plätze gingen ebenfalls an Systeme von Bull.
„Mit dem neuen System können wir den Energiebedarf für die Klimasimulationen unserer Nutzerinnen und Nutzer drastisch reduzieren. Für ein Rechenzentrum, dessen Aufgabe die Unterstützung bei der Erforschung des Klimas ist, ist das kein zusätzlicher Vorteil – es ist Teil unseres Auftrags“, sagte Dr. Hendryk Bockelmann, Abteilungsleiter Anwendungen am DKRZ.
„Wir sind stolz darauf, unsere langjährige Zusammenarbeit mit dem DKRZ, einem der führenden Klimarechenzentren Europas, fortzusetzen. HLRE-5 baut auf jahrelanger gemeinsamer Innovationsarbeit im Bereich des energieeffizienten Supercomputings auf und zeigt, wie moderne digitale Infrastruktur exzellente Klimaforschung unterstützen kann“, ergänzte Dr. Martin Matzke, Head of Northern and Central Europe bei Bull.
HLRE-5 besteht aus zwei Partitionen: einer GPU-Partition, die auf Superchips des Typs NVIDIA GB200 Grace Blackwell basiert und den Großteil der Simulations- und KI-Leistung des Systems bereitstellt, sowie einer CPU-Partition auf Basis von NVIDIA Vera-CPUs. Diese bringt erstmals die ARM-Architektur in das Kernsystem des DKRZ und verbessert die Energieeffizienz für Rechenaufgaben, die nicht auf GPUs ausgeführt werden, erheblich. Alle Rechnerknoten sind über NVIDIA Quantum-2-InfiniBand vernetzt. Diese Netzwerktechnologie ermöglicht die Kommunikation zwischen den Knoten mit geringer Latenz und hoher Datenrate (400 GBit/s), auf die globale Klimamodelle mit einer Auflösung im Kilometerbereich angewiesen sind.
„Wir sind NVIDIA für die langjährige Unterstützung bei der Optimierung von ICON für GPUs dankbar, die auch dazu beigetragen hat, dass wir 2025 den ACM Gordon Bell Prize for Climate Modelling gewonnen haben. Wir freuen uns darauf, diese Zusammenarbeit auf HLRE-5 fortzusetzen“, betonte Dr. Jan Frederik Engels, Mitglied des Gordon-Bell-Teams und Systemdesigner für den HPC-Teil des HLRE-5.
Beim Datenspeicher geht eine neue Strategie über die Kapazität als primären Maßstab für die Dimensionierung hinaus und konzentriert sich stattdessen auf die effiziente Nutzung von Ressourcen durch intelligente Datenplatzierung und die Verteilung auf unterschiedliche Speicherhierarchien. Im Mittelpunkt steht die neue IBM Storage-Scale-System-6000, das 60 Petabytes Festplattenspeicher mit einem Datendurchsatz von bis zu 340 Gigabytes/s mit einem dedizierten Flash-Speicher mit 500 Terabytes kombiniert. In enger Zusammenarbeit mit IBM können fortschrittliche Funktionen zur bedarfsgesteuerten Verteilung der Daten auf die Speicherhierarchien sowie die Nutzung der Speicherressourcen für unterschiedliche Forschungsaufgaben analysiert und weiter optimiert werden.
Der Flash-Speicher adressiert die rasant wachsenden Anforderungen der KI und ist dafür konzipiert, die für anspruchsvolle KI-Anwendungen erforderliche Leistung bereitzustellen. Zusammen mit der Größe und Effizienz der kapazitätsorientierten Speicherhierarchien bietet sie der Forschungsgemeinschaft eine leistungsstarke Grundlage sowohl für HPC als auch für die nächste Generation KI-gestützter Forschung.
Wie bei den Vorgängergenerationen setzt das DKRZ zur Kühlung des Systems auf die patentierte Direct-Liquid-Cooling-Technologien (DLC) von Bull. Dabei fließt warmes Wasser in einem geschlossenen Kreislauf durch die Rechnerknoten und führt die Wärme wesentlich effizienter ab als eine Luftkühlung.
Seit mehreren Jahren liefert das DKRZ einen Teil dieser Wärme an den benachbarten Fachbereich Chemie der Universität Hamburg. Mit der Installation von HLRE-5 wird die Kühlinfrastruktur modernisiert, sodass ein größerer Anteil der Abwärme zur weiteren Nutzung zur Verfügung steht. Die Universität Hamburg plant, diese Nutzung auf weitere Gebäude auf und rund um den KlimaCampus auszuweiten.
Die Gesamtinvestition in das System beträgt 40 Millionen Euro und umfasst einen fünfjährigen Supportvertrag. Die Finanzierung erfolgt hauptsächlich durch die Helmholtz-Gemeinschaft, die Max-Planck-Gesellschaft und die Stadt Hamburg im Rahmen der langfristigen Finanzierungsvereinbarung für die HPC-Systeme am DKRZ. Dank zusätzlicher Mittel der Max-Planck-Gesellschaft und des Bundesministeriums für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt im Rahmen der Hightech Agenda Deutschland (HTAD) konnte das System nochmals deutlich vergrößert werden.

Plakat der Winter Talks 2026

Die internationale Vortragsreihe "Winter Talks" des Fachbereichs Architektur der Hochschule Bochum lädt in diesem Semester dazu ein, Ordnung und Mehrdeutigkeit in der Architektur neu zu betrachten.
Ordnung und Mehrdeutigkeit lassen sich als komplementäre Bedingungen begreifen, die es der Architektur ermöglichen, zugleich lesbar und offen zu bleiben. Im Zentrum der Vortragsreihe steht die Frage, wie architektonische Ordnung durch Struktur, Geometrie und Bewegung, Lesbarkeit und Stabilität erzeugen kann – und zugleich wie Mehrdeutigkeit durch komplexe Gestaltung Räume für verschiedene Nutzungen und Interpretationen öffnet. Die diesjährige Vortragsreihe versteht Architektur als einen Zustand, in dem eine geordnete Struktur Raum für Ungewissheit, Wandel und Pluralität bietet.
Die Veranstaltungen finden in englischer Sprache statt.
Beginn jeweils donnerstags, 18:00 Uhr
Blue Box Auditorium, Am Hochschulcampus 1, D-44801 Bochum
Kuratiert von @professurkinzelbach, ENBK Entwerfen und Baukonstruktion
Unterstützt durch: BDA Bochum
05.11.2026: OFFICE Kersten Geers David Van Severen, Brüssel
David Van Severen: Massstab und Perspektive
OFFICE ist ein in Brüssel ansässiges Architekturbüro, das 2002 von Kersten Geers und David Van Severen gegründet wurde. Es dient als Plattform, um Architektur im Kontext der zeitgenössischen Kultur und des urbanen Umfelds zu erforschen und entwickeln. Die Projekte, unterschiedlich in Maßstab und Typologie, sind zugleich pragmatisch und innovativ; sie sind tief in verschiedenen architektonischen Traditionen verwurzelt und schaffen einen Rahmen, in dem sich das Leben in all seiner Komplexität entfalten kann. Die internationale Tätigkeit des Büros, die unter anderem mit dem Silbernen Löwen und dem Aga Khan Award for Architecture gewürdigt wurde, geht einher mit Forschungsarbeit, Publikationen und Lehrtätigkeiten.
19.11.2026: MADE arhitekti, Riga
Miķelis Putrāms: Struktur und Flexibilität
Das Schaffen von Architektur ist ein komplexer Prozess, der sowohl Struktur als auch Flexibilität erfordert. Das Büro MADE arhitekti unter der Leitung der Partner Linda Krūmiņa und Miķelis Putrāms hat Projekte für private Bauherren sowie öffentliche Aufträge mit Präzision und Engagement umgesetzt. Gebäude bringen einen gestalterischen Ansatz zum Ausdruck – doch noch wichtiger ist, dass sie unser Verhalten prägen. Flexibilität wird somit zu einem wirkungsvollen Instrument, um sowohl das Gebäude selbst als auch den Prozess seiner Entstehung zu steuern.
26.11.2026: ADEPT, Copenhagen
Simon Lyager Poulsen: Was wir nicht wissen, dass wir es nicht wissen
Indem sie soziale und urbane Synergien fördern, zeichnen sich die Entwürfe von ADEPT als „anti-ikonische“ Typologien aus – konzipiert als Rahmen für das Leben, fest verankert im jeweiligen Kontext, am menschlichen Maßstab orientiert und auf einen verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit Ressourcen ausgerichtet. Anstatt für eine festgelegte Zukunft zu planen, nähert sich das Büro seinen Entwürfen über Szenarien und offene Fragestellungen; dabei werden architektonische Ideen mit der Fähigkeit zur Anpassung, Aneignung und Veränderung in Einklang gebracht. Auf diese Weise schafft das Büro Gebäude und Orte, die nicht nur das aufnehmen können, was wir bereits kennen, sondern auch das, was wir heute noch nicht vorhersehen können.

title: Giga Storage secures financing, grid connection for 1.4 GWh CATL BESS project in Germany - Energy Storage
content: Giga Storage has closed financing for its large-scale “Albatross” battery energy storage system near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany. A consortium of seven banks is providing the Dutch developer with €260 million ($281 million) in debt capital for the project. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, while commissioning is planned for early 2029. The project will have a power output of 350 MW and capacity of 1.4 GWh, with a four-hour duration. The grid connection agreement with Amprion has also been signed. Commissioning is now scheduled for early 2029. The participating lenders in the financing round are ABN Amro, Hamburg Commercial Bank, ING, Rabobank, Siemens Financial Services via Siemens Bank, SMBC, and Société Générale. Giga Storage had previously announced in early October that the project had reached ready-to-build status. At that time, the company still expected the final investment decision in the fourth quarter, and commissioning was originally slated for 2028. Meanwhile, Giga Storage also signed a grid connection agreement with German transmission system operator (TSO) Amprion, and the agreement was concluded on October 14. Amprion stated that this marks the company’s first grid connection contract for a large-scale battery storage facility. The system will be connected directly to the 380 kV transmission grid at the Merzen substation. The storage facility will consist of 264 battery containers, 96 medium-voltage transformers, and two high-voltage transformers. According to Giga Storage, CATL will handle the engineering, construction, and maintenance of the facility, working alongside several European subcontractors. “Albatross” is Giga Storage’s first utility-scale storage project in Germany. Together with its “Leopard” project in the Netherlands and the “Green Turtle” project in Belgium, the company states that it currently has storage projects with a combined output of around 1.4 GW and a total capacity of 5.6 GWh under construction. title: Trina Storage to supply 196 MWh battery system for Japan's Nozu project - Energy Storage
content: Trina Storage, the battery energy storage business of China’s Trinasolar, has been selected to supply battery storage systems for the 50 MW/196 MWh AEJ Nozu project in Oita Prefecture, Japan. The company announced the contract on October 14, with project completion scheduled for the third quarter of 2028. Located in Nishihata, Nozu Town, Usuki City, the grid-scale facility will have a nominal storage duration of approximately 3.9 hours. It is being developed by Nozomi Energy, a Japanese renewable energy platform backed by infrastructure investor Actis, through its project company AEJ Nozu Storage Power Plant Contract Company. The project secured a capacity contract in Japan’s fiscal 2023 Long-Term Decarbonization Auction, providing inflation-linked capacity payments over 20 years. Nozomi Energy reached financial close in September 2026 after securing non-recourse project financing from Japan’s Aozora Bank. The financing amount has not been disclosed. China Energy Engineering Shanxi Electric Power Engineering Co., Ltd. has separately secured the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the project’s balance-of-plant works. The company said the development had obtained key land and grid-connection permits. Trina Storage will supply its Elementa 2 Pro battery energy storage solution, built around standardized 5 MWh containerized units. According to the manufacturer’s technical documentation, the system uses its proprietary 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, with a nominal energy capacity of 5.015 MWh per container and a DC voltage architecture approaching 1,500 V. The system is housed in a standard 20-foot high-cube container and incorporates liquid cooling, battery monitoring and multiple layers of safety protection. Trina Storage says its thermal management design maintains cell temperature differences within 2.5 C, while the system features IP67-rated battery modules and an IP55-rated enclosure. Additional safety features include temperature and smoke monitoring, active ventilation and fire suppression systems. Trina Storage specifies a cell cycle life of up to 12,000 cycles for the product, although the company has not disclosed project-specific operating assumptions or performance guarantees for the Nozu installation. The manufacturer said its Japanese operations will support system configuration, technical consultation, delivery coordination and after-sales services, working with local project partners to address technical and regulatory requirements. “For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities,” said Leo Zhao, head of energy storage for Asia-Pacific at Trina Storage. The contract adds to Trina Storage’s Japanese project portfolio, which includes a separate 160 MWh utility-scale BESS in the Kyushu region. In September, the company also signed a memorandum of understanding with Japanese developer AMP-lify covering approximately 1 GWh of potential grid-connected storage projects using its newer Elementa 3 series. Nozu is among the battery storage developments supported by Japan’s long-term decarbonization capacity mechanism, which is intended to encourage investment in low-carbon generation and flexible power resources. The project’s long-term contracted capacity revenue provides greater revenue visibility for its developer, while construction, equipment delivery and commissioning remain ahead of its planned 2028 completion. The value of Trina Storage’s supply contract and the project’s total investment cost have not been disclosed. title: Samsung SDI signs 1 GWh supply agreement for US-made NCA battery storage - Energy Storage
content: Samsung SDI has signed a deal to supply 1 GWh of nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) battery storage to a single US customer, with all cells and modules to be manufactured in the United States. Under the agreement with utility and independent power producer Alpha Omega Power (APO), Samsung SDI is expected to deliver its Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7 containerized energy storage to projects scheduled to being construction in 2027. These will include projects in the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) energy markets. All cells and modules for the  battery containers covered in the supply agreement will be manufactured at Samsung SDI’s StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in Kokomo, Indiana, according to the manufacturer, with delivery expected before the end of 2026. In choosing Samsung SDI as a supplier, APO is putting significant investment into NCA chemistry battery storage in a global market where cells using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) based chemistry continue to lead. The investment also comes as the US government mulls further restrictions on imported power equipment. Samsung SDI reports that the SBB 1.7 uses a high-nickel NCA chemistry and delivers 17% higher energy density than its predecessor, the SBB 1.5, while maintaining the same 20-foot footprint. The manufacturer also highlights fire safety as a key feature of the design, noting the battery storage solution incorporates Samsung SDI’s proprietary Enhanced Direct Injection technology, which directly injects fire-extinguishing agents into individual battery modules. The latest agreement means Samsung SDI has been contracted to supply a total of 1.5 GWh of energy storage to APO, following an earlier supply contract signed in 2025. In a press release, Fabrice Hudry president ESS of Samsung SDI America, said the company’s “differentiated technology” and US production capabilities will see it continue to expand in the North American ESS market. Paul Choi, CEO of Alpha Omega Power, added: “American-made ESS from Samsung SDI will play an important role in AOP’s continued growth. title: Spain announces 27 renewable projects with 1.78 GW of BESS - Energy Storage
content: Spain published announcements for 27 renewable energy projects involving BESS in the third quarter of 2026, including standalone battery installations and projects combining storage with existing solar and wind farms. Among the largest projects is Jinko Power Energy’s proposed 150.8 MW BESS La Puebla 3 in Cerro de Andévalo, Huelva, which would be integrated with the existing La Puebla 3 solar park. FRV also submitted announcements for BESS Gaetana, a 108 MW battery system intended to be combined with a 166.4 MW solar plant in Badajoz to form a 180 MW hybrid installation, and BESS Aurea, a 117.6 MW battery system for an existing 171 MW solar plant in the same province. FRV’s other announcement covers the 49.94 MW BESS Camarreal project in Camargo. Several announcements concern battery systems being added to existing solar installations. Solaria’s projects include the 45 MW Maira Gamma battery system, paired with a 140.127 MW solar installation in Burgos; a 19.993 MW system at Solaria-Tordesillas II in Valladolid; and a 31 MW Pegaso battery system, also in Valladolid, intended for the 77.35 MW Pegaso Solar installation. Solaria also announced the 22.26 MW Talayuela II BESS project in Cáceres, which would be combined with an existing 44.55 MW solar plant to form a 66.81 MW hybrid installation. Bruc Energy’s announcements cover multiple battery systems in Seville province. These include the 39.6 MW Freya system, paired with an existing 44 MW solar park in Carmona; the 39.6 MW Artemisa and Elvisa systems, each intended for an existing 46.2 MW solar park in Alcalá de Guadaíra; the 28.37 MW Bianor system, paired with a 33 MW solar park in Utrera; and four further 39.6 MW systems named SES, Jade, Esmeralda and Heracles, each intended for an existing 46.2 MW solar park in Alcalá de Guadaíra. Other solar-linked projects include Opdenergy’s 24.04 MW OPDE Miramundo system in Puerto Real, Cádiz, for an existing 49.99 MW solar plant, and its 26.74 MW Hibridación Larral project in Zaragoza, intended for an existing 40 MW solar installation. Ignis announced the 21.6 MW MGE Almacenamiento Mulhacén system for a 70 MW solar plant in Toledo, as well as two battery systems at Azor Solar in the Madrid region, rated at 23.898 MW and 44.614 MW, for a 64.02 MW solar plant. Sonnedix’s 40 MW BESS Los Frailes project in Badajoz would be paired with a 40.25 MW solar plant. Additional announcements cover projects from Enel Green, X-Elio, Grenergy, Dargon Energy and other developers. Enel Green’s 41.58 MW BESS Mudéjar project in Teruel would be combined with the 66 MW Mudéjar-Millán Hernández Bonaga solar park; the same announcement also rejected preliminary administrative authorization for a proposed 75 MW San Jorge wind module. X-Elio’s 83.709 MW La Atalaya battery project in Villena, Alicante, is intended for the 96.884 MW La Atalaya solar plant. Grenergy’s announcements cover the 21.69 MW Aspe and Aitana battery systems, each intended for an existing 49.11 MW solar installation in Cuenca. Dargon Energy’s PHFV Castellet project is a 4.99 MW storage installation in Catalonia. Several projects would combine batteries with wind power or with existing hybrid renewable energy facilities. EDP’s 19.5 MW Castillo Garcimuñoz battery system in Cuenca would be integrated with an existing 25.5 MW wind farm and a 20.925 MW hybrid solar installation, forming a 30 MW hybrid facility. Iberdrola announced a 35 MW battery system for the 44.681 MW Virgen de Areños III solar plant in Palencia, as well as a 30.3 MW battery system for the 70.4 MW Iglesias wind farm in Burgos. RIC Energy’s 21.6 MW BESS system would be added to the 24.035 MW Greencar 3 hybrid installation in Carmona, Seville. Statkraft’s Talayuela II project is among the announcements for battery systems integrated with existing solar facilities. Elawan’s 20 MW Frontones Phase II storage project in Albacete would be added to an existing complex comprising a 50 MW wind farm, a 26.25 MW hybrid solar plant and a 4 MW storage installation, forming a hybrid facility with a stated capacity of 60 MW. Benbros announced the 49.738 MW BESS Solorzano project in Cantabria. The announcements cover different stages of the administrative process, including applications for preliminary administrative authorization and construction authorization, environmental assessment and declarations of public utility. Publication of an announcement does not necessarily mean that a project has secured all required permits or will proceed to construction. The published list identifies the initial promoters of the projects. Some may have since been sold or transferred. title: Servotech launches single-phase hybrid solar inverters for residential applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Servotech Renewable Power System has unveiled its Sparkle Pro IP54 single-phase hybrid solar inverters for residential applications. The range comprises 3 kW, 4.2 kW and 6 kW models.
The inverters manage solar power generation, battery storage (lithium-ion or lead-acid) and grid supply through a single system. The 3 kW and 4.2 kW models operate with 24 V DC battery systems, while the 6 kW model uses a 48 V DC battery configuration.
The inverters support a maximum PV input voltage of 500 V and feature a built-in maximum power point tracking (MPPT) solar charge controller, with an MPPT operating voltage range of 40–500 V. They are compatible with both lithium-ion and lead-acid batteries. Additional features include lithium battery activation using PV or utility power.
Designed with an IP54-rated enclosure, the Sparkle Pro series offers protection against dust ingress and water splashes. Other features include RS232, RS485, USB and dry-contact interfaces, an LED display, grid-feed-in capability and a noise-control algorithm.

title: Researchers develop photovoltaic-thermal collector with wavy copper cooling tubes - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers at Razi University in Iran have investigated how the geometry of copper cooling tubes affects the electrical and thermal performance of photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) collectors. They aimed to determine whether wavy tubes could improve heat extraction and boost overall system efficiency compared with conventional straight tubes. To this end, they experimentally assessed three tube configurations at different water flow rates.
“This study presents an experimental investigation into the performance of a water-cooled PVT system integrated with wavy copper channels, aiming to quantify the impact of channel geometry and flow rate on thermal and electrical efficiencies,” the researchers said. “Notably, unlike many small-scale studies, this research is conducted on a commercially representative PV module.”
The researchers built a water-cooled PVT collector using a 180 W PV module measuring 68 cm × 148 cm, with an aluminum absorber plate attached to its rear side. They fabricated three copper-tube cooling assemblies: one with straight tubes and two with mechanically bent wavy tubes featuring pitches of 200 mm and 300 mm, respectively, and a wave height of 50 mm. They used silicone thermal paste to improve thermal contact between the tubes and the absorber plate, while copper strips and thermally conductive adhesive secured the assemblies.
The team conducted outdoor tests in Kermanshah, western Iran, in May 2025, under an average ambient temperature of 27 C and solar irradiance of 1,038 W/m2. Each configuration was tested at water flow rates ranging from 200 mL/min to 800 mL/min, with the inlet water temperature maintained at 20 C. The researchers also tested an uncooled PV module for comparison. Each test lasted approximately 30 minutes, until operating conditions stabilized.
“The implementation of the liquid cooling effectively reduced the panel temperature,” the academics said. “In the optimal configuration tested of W-200 tube at 800mL⋅min 1, the absorber plate temperature was reduced to approximately 49 C, compared to 64 C in the uncooled system, a reduction of ∼15 C. Similarly, the uncooled panel surface temperature, which reached a maximum of nearly 67 C, was significantly mitigated.”
The researchers also found that the W-200 configuration, featuring a 200 mm pitch, achieved the highest electrical efficiency of 13.65% at a water flow rate of 800 mL/min, compared with 12.63% for the uncooled module. This represented an improvement of 1.02 percentage points.
The W-200 configuration also recorded the highest pressure drop, reaching approximately 1,200 Pa at a flow rate of 400 mL/min, compared with around 750 Pa for the straight-tube configuration at the same flow rate.
“The W-200 tube exhibited the most effective heat extraction among the tested cases, achieving a maximum thermal efficiency of approximately 24% at 800 mL · min-1, compared to just 18%for the straight tube,” the scientists said. “Consequently, the optimal W-200 configuration delivered a maximum overall efficiency exceeding 37%, substantially outperforming the straight tube with ∼31%.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Experimental analysis of thermal performance of a photovoltaic – thermal hybrid solar collector (PVT) with wavy channel
,” published in
Energy Nexus

title: INA Solar, Caelux target perovskite-silicon tandem module production by 2028 - pv magazine Global
content:
Insolation Energy Ltd.
(INA Solar), through its subsidiary Insolation Green Energy, has signed a five-year strategic partnership agreement with US-based
Caelux Corp.
to commercialize 3 GW of solar modules integrating Caelux’s power-generating glass technology with INA Solar’s n-type TOPCon platform.
The companies plan to develop high-efficiency hybrid-tandem solar modules, targeting commercial production with module efficiencies of up to 29% by 2028.
Under the agreement, INA Solar and Caelux will collaborate on technology validation, manufacturing readiness and regulatory approvals, including compliance with India’s Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) requirements.
“By combining advanced perovskite technology with our TOPCon manufacturing capabilities, we aim to accelerate the development of high-efficiency solar modules and contribute to India’s renewable energy ambitions,” said Manish Gupta, chairman of Insolation Energy.
Vikas Jain, managing director of Insolation Energy, said the partnership would strengthen the company’s efforts to build an integrated solar manufacturing ecosystem.
Scott Graybeal, CEO of Caelux, said the agreement represents a step toward commercializing next-generation solar technology at scale in India. With the latest agreement, Caelux’s total contracted volume with module manufacturers worldwide exceeds 25 GW.
“Integrating Energy Producing Glass with TOPCon technology represents a significant step towards the Indian market benefiting from ultra-high power density solar modules,” said Vish Iyer, Caelux’s managing director for India and West Asia.
INA Solar operates three solar module manufacturing facilities in Jaipur, Rajasthan, with a combined annual production capacity of 5.5 GW. The company is also developing a 4.5 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility and an aluminum frame manufacturing plant with an annual capacity of 18,000 metric tons in Narmadapuram, Madhya Pradesh.
Its product portfolio includes TOPCon and monocrystalline PERC modules rated from 500 W to 635 W. The company also provides engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) services and has an independent power producer (IPP) portfolio of approximately 400 MW.
Founded in 2015 and headquartered in Jaipur, Insolation Energy is listed on India’s National Stock Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). The company operates across more than 250 districts in India and reports more than 40,000 customers and a network of over 1,000 channel partners.
Caelux has also partnered with Indian solar manufacturer Grew Solar to develop
4 GW of perovskite-silicon tandem module production capacity
. Under the five-year agreement announced in September 2026, Grew Solar will integrate Caelux’s perovskite-coated glass with its n-type TOPCon technology, including its large-format G12R module series.
The companies are targeting module efficiencies of at least 29%, with commercial production expected to begin in 2028. Caelux has also signed separate agreements with Rayzon Solar and Navitas Solar to develop a combined 10 GW of hybrid-tandem module capacity in India, with production similarly targeted for 2028.

title: TCL SunPower launches 505 W back-contact solar panel with 24.7% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
TCL SunPower
, a unit of Chinese PV manufacturer
TCL Zhonghuan
, has introduced its new SunPower Origin solar panel series for residential rooftop applications.
“The module format offers significant advantages, particularly on rooftops that are not perfectly rectangular or have obstacles such as chimneys,” the company’s Director of Product Management, Karin Alberto-Burkhardt, told
pv magazine
. “Its dimensions allow installers to fit more modules compared with conventional panels.”
The new modules are based on the manufacturer’s eighth-generation back-contact cell technology and feature a fully black design. They are available in five versions, with power outputs ranging from 485 W to 505 W and efficiencies between 23.8% and 24.7%.
The SPR-BE54-HD505, the most powerful module in the series, delivers 505 W and achieves a maximum efficiency of 24.7%. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.88 V and its short-circuit current is 15.58 A. The module has a maximum power voltage of 34.08 V and a maximum power current of 14.82 A.
The smallest panel in the series, the SPR-BE54-HD485, has a power output of 485 W and an efficiency of 23.8%. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.45 V and its short-circuit current is 15.18 A.
All five modules measure 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weigh 26.0 kg. They feature 2mm + 2 mm semi-tempered glass, a black anodized aluminum frame and an IP68-rated junction box with three bypass diodes. The modules have a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 70 C.
The panels have a temperature coefficient of -0.26%/C for power, a voltage temperature coefficient of -0.22%/C and a current temperature coefficient of 0.05%/C. Their maximum series fuse rating is 30 A.
According to the manufacturer, the back-contact cells are patterned using lithography rather than laser processing, which the company claims reduces the risk of microcracks.
TCL SunPower Global also said the modules are designed to improve performance under partial shading. The company claims that the electrical architecture of the 54-cell panel provides shading behavior equivalent to more than 16,000 bypass diodes, helping limit localized heating and maintain power generation in unshaded areas.
The technology has received a Class A+ shading-resistance certification from TÜV Rheinland, according to the manufacturer. The modules are certified to IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 standards and have a Class C fire rating under IEC 61730-2 and UL 790. They have also undergone ammonia, dust and sand, and salt mist testing.
The manufacturer offers a 40-year warranty covering the product, power output and service. It guarantees at least 99% of nominal output after the first year, with maximum annual degradation of 0.25% thereafter. Based on these warranty terms, the guaranteed output after 40 years is approximately 89.25% of the initial rated power.
TCL SunPower Global said its historical installed base of more than 15 GW of back-contact modules has recorded a warranty return rate of 0.005%, based on an internal analysis conducted in June 2026.
Alongside the residential series, the company has introduced a commercial version of SunPower Origin featuring 66 back-contact cells. The bifacial module measures 2,192 mm × 1,134 mm, delivers up to 615 W and offers bifaciality of up to 80%, according to the manufacturer.
“We are targeting bifaciality levels of up to 85%,” Alberto-Burkhardt said. “The improved power density and module format also allow installers to fit more panels on commercial rooftops. These are important advantages when roof geometry and available space limit system design,”
The new panels are available for ordering through TCL SunPower Partners across Europe, with initial deliveries expected before the end of 2026.

title: 5B pre-fab solar tech gets nod for 70 MW project in Australia - pv magazine Global
content:
Modular solar specialist 5B has executed a purchase order with 1414 Degrees to deliver 70 MW of its prefabricated
Maverick solar units
for the initial stage of the Aurora Energy Precinct project being developed in South Australia’s Upper Spencer Gulf region.
The Aurora project, planned for a 16 km² site near Port Augusta, combines large-scale solar generation potential with battery energy storage and proposed grid connections to supply firmed renewable power to the National Electricity Market (NEM) and behind the meter to data centres and other major energy users.
The initial 70 MW solar PV development forms part of Aurora’s Stage 1 project, alongside an
approved 140 MW / 280 MWh battery
energy storage system (BESS).
Adelaide-based 1414 Degrees, which was originally founded as a long-duration thermal energy storage (TES) company, said 5B’s technology was selected for its compact layout, which promises to accommodate more solar capacity per hectare, supporting the Aurora project’s potential for about 2 GW of PV capacity.
“The Maverick layout allows us to accommodate considerably more solar capacity within the available land, supporting staged expansion alongside storage, connection infrastructure and customer demand,” 1414 Degrees Executive Chairman Kevin Moriarty said.
The Maverick system is a ground-mounted solar array of up to 90 pre-wired PV panels that are fitted to frames that can be unfolded accordion style. The frames come preassembled on concrete blocks that replace conventional mounting structures, allowing for rapid installation on site. 5B said the solar panels, cabling and connections are factory-assembled and tested before transport to site, which reduces on-site assembly work.
The initial 70 MW deployment will cover 42 hectares within Aurora’s approved 200-hectare solar development footprint. 1414 Degrees said its assessment indicates the Maverick layout could accommodate more than 300 MW of solar PV capacity across that footprint and “supports the indicative precinct-wide potential of approximately 2 GW of solar PV capacity.”
5B said the Maverick units for the Aurora project will be manufactured at the company’s production facility in Adelaide and transported to the precinct for installation.
Moriarty said the execution of the purchase order is a major milestone for the Aurora project.
“Placing this order is a further step towards delivery of Aurora’s initial 70 MW solar development,” he said, adding that the company is now “progressing power purchase agreements, infrastructure partnerships and financing for project delivery.”
1414 Degrees, which assumed full ownership of the Aurora project earlier this year, said it has already secured approval from the Australian Energy Market Operator for connection of the 140 MW / 280 MWh BESS and commercial transmission access negotiations for the proposed 275 kV connection are advancing.
The company is also progressing a proposed 33 kV connection pathway to support earlier data centre development and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.
In July, 1414 Degrees entered into a heads of agreement with an unidentified Australian data centre operator for the proposed development of up to 1 GW of AI data centre infrastructure at Aurora.

title: Emmvee unveils TOPCon module with four-cut cell design - pv magazine Global
content:
Indian PV manufacturer Emmvee has unveiled a TOPCon solar module featuring a four-cut cell design at Renewable Energy India Expo (REI) 2026. The module delivers 640–650 W, 25–30 W more power than conventional half-cut modules of the same dimensions, according to the company. Emmvee also showcased a 2,000 V DC solar module aimed at reducing balance-of-system costs.
The quarter-cut TOPCon module has each solar cell divided into four sections, compared with the two sections used in conventional half-cut modules.
Each section carries one quarter of the module current, reducing resistive losses in the cell interconnections. The module also uses cell overlap, or negative cell placement, to improve space utilisation and increase power output without increasing module dimensions, according to Emmvee.
The module is designed with a lower temperature coefficient. This means the module loses less power as its temperature rises, helping maintain higher power output in hot conditions. The design is also expected to reduce heat generated within the module during operation. Another benefit is the improved performance under shading. The smaller cell sections help limit the area affected by shading and hotspots and thereby allowing the module to maintain approximately 85% performance compared with 75% for conventional modules.
Also, over the longer term, the new module is engineered to retain its power-generating capacity better. Typically, half-cut modules have a power degradation rate of 1% in the first year and 0.4% annually from the second year onwards. The quad-cut module has a degradation rate of 0.35% in the corresponding time frame. It is designed to retain the same general electrical specification class as the existing half-cut product, according to Emmvee.
Emmvee’s 2,000 V DC PV module allows more modules to be connected in each string, reducing the number of strings, cables, trenches and electrical components required across a project.  This lowers installation time, labour requirements and balance-of-system costs. By carrying the same power at lower current, it also reduces energy losses that happens on DC cables, helping more of the electricity generated by the modules reach the grid. “The new module requires fewer inverters, and combiner boxes simplifying plant design and maintenance. In fact, it helps lower the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) by 1.8%,” stated the company.

title: 科学网-西北大学获批设立“金丝猴国家保护研究中心”
content:
西北大学获批设立“金丝猴国家保护研究中心”
记者10月26日从西北大学获悉，该校正式获批设立“金丝猴国家保护研究中心”。该中心聚焦金丝猴这一旗舰物种，着力建设集“科学研究、救护繁育、科普宣传、人才培养、国际合作”于一体的国家综合创新平台，打造金丝猴保护研究的“国家队”和“排头兵”。
长期以来，西北大学生命科学学院教授李保国带领团队，深耕秦岭生物多样性保护与灵长类动物研究，建设了国际首个金丝猴野外观测研究基地，还与中国科学院动物研究所共建陕西秦岭大熊猫金丝猴生物多样性国家野外科学观测研究站。学校在金丝猴的生态学、行为学、遗传学以及秦岭生态监测、保护与生态恢复实践等领域取得了一系列具有国际影响力的原创性成果。前期完善的野外观测体系以及多学科交叉的科研优势，为中心的成功获批奠定了坚实基础。
记者了解到，金丝猴国家保护研究中心将与湖北、四川、贵州、云南、甘肃以及陕西省相关动物保护主管部门、自然保护区和繁育中心等机构紧密合作，逐步形成“中心—分中心+野外台站—繁育野化基地”协同发展的布局，力争产出一批具有国际领先水平的重大科研成果，推动我国灵长类动物保护研究水平走向世界前列。
金丝猴国家保护研究中心由国家林业和草原局与陕西省人民政府合作共建，被列入西安区域科技创新中心建设任务，实行“局省共建、校地协同”机制，致力于全面提升我国金丝猴保护研究水平。

title: 科学网-他53岁丢掉名校教职，5年后诽谤案胜诉
content:
他53岁丢掉名校教职，5年后诽谤案胜诉
等待陪审团裁决的那几个小时，现年58岁的细胞生物学家David Sabatini形容为“一生中最令人神经紧绷的时刻”。
2026年10月16日，结果出炉。美国马萨诸塞州萨福克县高等法院的陪审团裁定， Sabatini起诉前同事Kristin Knouse诽谤一案胜诉，Knouse需赔偿600万美元；她提出的性骚扰反诉，被全部驳回。
这位前美国麻省理工学院（MIT）生物学家随后在社交平台上说，这是他5年多来第一次真正露出笑容。
2021年，一纸调查结论，将正值事业巅峰的他拽入舆论漩涡。那时，作为mTOR信号通路的重要发现者，Sabatini顶着美国国家科学院院士头衔，在实验室深耕二十余年，被外界视作诺贝尔奖有力竞争者。指控袭来之后，他接连失去研究所、基金会的岗位，在美国高校求职屡屡碰壁。他的科研事业近乎崩塌。
如今，判决在生命科学圈激起巨大涟漪。一边是陪审团的司法裁决，一边是此前学术机构的调查认定。两种结论，两种叙事，摆在整个科研共同体面前。
Sabatini。图源：个人官网
“人人避之不及的人物”
在风波到来之前，Sabatini的履历堪称学术界范本。
博士阶段，他就找到了雷帕霉素的作用靶点mTOR。这条通路掌管细胞生长、代谢、增殖，关联癌症、衰老、糖尿病等诸多重大疾病。1997年，年仅29岁的他就在美国怀特黑德研究所独立建立实验室；2002年入职MIT；2008年拿下了含金量极高的霍华德·休斯医学研究所（HHMI）研究员职位；2016年，48岁的他当选美国国家科学院院士。
二十余年间，他的实验室产出大量高水平成果，多篇重磅论文发表在顶级期刊，走出了近50位独立PI。他还创办了数家生物技术公司。
然而，崩塌往往只在瞬息之间。
Knouse是一名由哈佛大学与MIT联合培养的医学博士-哲学博士在读生。在她求学期间，Sabatini是她的授课教师之一，并且是能决定她学术命运的学位论文委员会成员。后来，Knouse以研究员的身份加入了怀特黑德研究所，正准备建立属于自己的实验室。就在那段时间，两人发生了性关系。
这段关系的性质，成为日后风暴的中心。现任MIT生物学助理教授的Knouse表示，自己当时遭到了Sabatini的胁迫。而Sabatini则坚称，一切皆是自愿。
2021年，怀特黑德研究所对员工的一次常规调查，意外把线索引向了Sabatini实验室。研究所随即聘请了外部律所展开深度调查。结论是致命的：调查认定Sabatini违反了研究所的自愿交往关系政策以及反骚扰政策。不仅如此，报告还指出，他营造了一种充满性暗示的实验室环境，并且在调查期间试图误导调查人员、左右受访人员的证词。
一连串严重后果接踵而至。Sabatini被HHMI解雇；同时被迫辞去怀特黑德研究所的职务，亲手关闭了自己苦心经营的实验室。在3名高级管理人员建议撤销其终身教职后，这位曾经的学术巨擘黯然辞去了MIT的教授一职。
正如他的代理律师Lisa Arrowood所言，这些指控让这位曾经前程似锦的生物学家，“在科学界彻底沦为人人避之不及的人物”。
学术机构的调查画上句号，但属于法庭的较量，才刚刚拉开序幕。
600万美元的“清白”与罗生门
跌入谷底后，Sabatini选择了反击。2021年10月，他正式提起诉讼。被告名单包含Kristin Knouse、怀特黑德研究所以及时任所长Ruth Lehmann，起诉理由包含诽谤、性别歧视等多项诉求。
这场官司，打了整整5年。除了判赔600万美元，陪审团还一并驳回了Knouse提出的性骚扰以及打击报复的反诉。
陪审团作出裁决后，Sabatini在社交平台发表感言，表示5年多来首次真正露出笑容。
对Sabatini来说，这代表着“彻底的清白昭雪”，让他获得了巨大解脱。他声称，自己是在为追求其他女性而结束二人关系之后，Knouse才提出了骚扰相关的指控。他的代理律师Arrowood也强调，Knouse当时已经拥有自己的实验室、独立的科研经费和手下学生，两人之间并不存在权力不对等，她只是一个“想要向前任恋人实施报复的人”。
但这个结果，却让许多法律专家感到意外。毕竟在此之前，Sabatini针对怀特黑德研究所及Ruth Lehmann发起的法律挑战均以失败告终。
专门处理性骚扰案件的律师Ann Olivarius直言：“这是一项分量极重的认定。很明显，陪审团作出了对她极为不利的裁决。”同时，她对如此高额的损害赔偿金感到惊讶，认为这种情况实属罕见，这是一个极具代表性的案件。在Olivarius看来，声称Sabatini对比自己年轻很多、尚处在职业早期的Knouse不具备权力优势的说法，简直“十分荒谬”。“看看他的身份地位，再看看她的处境……这根本就不是一段平等的关系。”
Knouse的代理律师Ellen Zucker告诉《科学》杂志，她的当事人打算对该判决提起上诉。“这份判决令人深感失望。”Zucker指出，在庭审中另有数名女性出庭作证，讲述了她们与Sabatini之间“令人不安的交往经历”。“令人痛心的是，陪审团的裁决完全没有考量这些证词。”
Zucker认为，要求一名处于职业生涯早期阶段的科学家承担600万美元的赔偿金，“恰恰证明陪审团并不具备为此案作出恰当裁决的能力，而他们确实也没有做到”。
Zucker表示：“我们这个时代一个令人悲哀的现实是，社会仍然难以相信女性，也难以体会她们面对那些往往掌控着她们命运的男性时所要承受的难处。”Zucker强调，Knouse已经走上法庭说出了真相，司法程序还没有走到终点。
这起民事诉讼的判决，在法律上对怀特黑德研究所当年的调查结论并没有直接约束力。但Sabatini及其支持者，已经将这份判决视作对他的洗冤。包括亿万富豪Bill Ackman在内的一部分人，开始公开呼吁该研究所重新审视此前的调查结论，并要求Lehmann辞职。Ackman不仅利用自己庞大的社交媒体网络为Sabatini发声，还资助了他近期的科研工作。
真相究竟如何？法庭上的胜负似乎并未终结这场罗生门。
2500万美元资助与一纸禁令
事实上，Ackman的支持并不是从判决后才开始的。在长达5年的诉讼里，丢掉了所有职位的Sabatini，一直在设法让实验重新运转起来。
2023年2月，转机出现。Ackman与一位匿名捐赠者共同承诺出资总计2500万美元，助力他重启实验室。同年晚些时候，Sabatini入职捷克科学院有机化学与生物化学研究所。为了更方便地开展研究，该研究所近期在波士顿地区设立了分支，Sabatini如今在那里拥有了第二处实验场地。
然而，旧日的阴影并未完全散去。
2024年，美国卫生与公众服务部（HHS）宣布，因相关指控，拟禁止他获取任何联邦科研资助。据《科学》杂志获悉，HHS下属机构美国国立卫生研究院已于2025年9月正式发出禁令，禁止Sabatini在一年内申请该机构的科研基金。对一个靠经费养实验室的生物学家来说，这又是一记重拳。
戏剧性的转折再次发生。根据Sabatini向《科学》杂志提供的一份来自HHS的邮件显示，这项禁令已于2026年4月提前解除。邮件给出的理由是，这名生物学家向该机构提交了补充材料。
与此同时，那场风波的余波依然在学术界回荡。2022年，纽约大学格罗斯曼医学院曾考虑过Sabatini的岗位遴选，但在学生与教职员工的强烈抗议声中，他最终退出了竞争。Sabatini始终否认自己在实验室营造了充满性暗示、“恶劣”的工作氛围。
判决下达之后，Sabatini接受《纽约时报》采访，言语之中满是感慨。
“长久以来，我一直期盼这一刻，但常常觉得自己或许撑不下去，无论是经济上、情绪上，还是身体上。”他形容这份判决如梦似幻，希望未来外界重新依据科研成果、育人经历评价自己；他期待条件合适的时候，能够再度回到MIT开展工作。
但这份胜诉，并不代表所有争议就此尘埃落定。
怀特黑德研究所迅速发布声明，指出Sabatini针对研究所的相关诉讼早已被法官驳回，本次庭审被告只有Sabatini与Knouse两人，机构本身并不参与本次判决，不代表推翻此前机构内部调查结果。MIT则没有对外就本次陪审团裁决给出公开回应。
这场横跨5年的风波，给全球科研共同体留下了几道难题：当导师与青年科研人员发生亲密关系时，权力不对等该如何界定？高校或机构内部职场调查应当建立怎样的程序边界？被指控的科研人员名誉受损后，又该如何讨回公道？
法槌已经落下，“清白”二字仍悬而未决。
